channel.title: Podcast — The world is too loud. Read what matters.
channel.description: Every day, the judgements worth remembering from 197 Chinese- and English-language podcasts. Points and quotes carry timestamps — tap one and you are back at the second it was said. Quotes are checked word for word and figures back to the source; anything unverifiable is cut, not published.

item.title: AI can now build a virus; the defense side is still stuck on sequence alignment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-latentspace-ai-能造出病毒了-防御方还停在序列比对/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-latentspace-ai-能造出病毒了-防御方还停在序列比对/
item.description: The models that generate pathogenic sequences and the models that tell whether a sequence is pathogenic are essentially the same models, so the teams doing design are best positioned to do defense — but the defense side is far behind, with a baseline still stuck at sequence matching.
item.content:encoded:
The models that generate pathogenic sequences and the models that tell whether a sequence is pathogenic are essentially the same models, so the teams doing design are best positioned to do defense — but the defense side is far behind, with a baseline still stuck at sequence matching.

High information density; the middle and later sections on the four layers of biodefense, the DNA synthesis pipeline, and "you can't patch a human" are the most valuable.

0:00 The teams doing design are best positioned to do defense
The dual mission Eric set for Radical Numerics is not a PR gesture but a technical judgment: the models that can generate pathogenic sequences and the models that can tell whether a sequence is pathogenic are essentially the same models. So the teams doing design are naturally best positioned to do defense, rather than outsourcing defense to a different group. He acknowledges there is an arms-race dynamic here, and that the defenders have always been far behind; what the company wants to do is pull the defenders up to the same level.

8:12 AI built the first genome from scratch
Evo's work generating a CRISPR-Cas system landed in Science, and Eric later gave a TED Talk. More important is what scientists showed last year: using a generative DNA model to generate the first genome from scratch. Humans had previously only been able to copy and paste fragments of known function, and had never built from scratch at the genome level. What Evo generated was a functional bacteriophage, that is, a virus. Eric says this is a turning point for the scientific community and the company — it means being able to build complete organisms that do not exist in nature, and with that, the corresponding potential for harm.

12:16 Omni's breakthrough came from alignment, not pretraining
Evo showed the potential of pretraining, but on human genetics it still lost to specialized DNA models, and the community questioned why one would use a large model at all. Omni's difference is mid-training and post-training: presenting tasks in the question-and-answer form scientists actually want, for example, given a wild-type and a mutant sequence, help me find the causal variant. Eric says this kind of form does not emerge naturally from pretraining. The results surprised them — Omni was not just competitive across many tasks the way Evo was, it began pushing the frontier in every subfield, especially variant effect prediction.

23:50 Most real disease variants are in non-coding regions
Traditional bioinformatics tools and statistical methods mainly focus on coding regions, and coding regions make up only about 1.5% to 2% of the genome. Eric says many, perhaps most, diseases actually fall in non-coding regulatory regions, where variants are harder to judge as pathogenic or not. This is exactly where Omni is strong: it can distinguish pathogenic mutations in non-coding regions, especially long-range ones. This is precisely what geneticists who have long been unable to use traditional tools want.

45:44 The biology experiment itself is doing the filtering
The mechanism of the SOLEX experiment is worth remembering: generate a large number of random sequences, turn them into aptamer switches, and read them out at high throughput with NGS — the more binding, the more reads, the higher the fitness; then mutate the winning sequences again and iterate. This experiment explored on the order of 10 to the 11th power sequences in parallel. The key is that "the biology of the experiment is actually doing the filtering" — the wet lab does the filtering, and the model reproduces that process in silico. This paradigm can be generalized to any biological experiment of "progressive refinement," as long as you can capture the intermediate states.

58:15 Stanford scientists said generating DNA was a stupid idea
Eric spent six months at Stanford on the idea of Evo "generating DNA," and almost every scientist he talked to thought it was a stupid idea. The objections were specific: humans themselves do not understand the rules of DNA, so why expect AI to learn them; you cannot even tell whether the generation is correct, so how do you give the model feedback; DNA has too many repetitive sequences, too noisy a distribution, no real rules, all junk. He admits he was just stubborn, felt "it just feels right," but at the time could not say what the use case was. The first time they trained Evo, they had no idea whether it would work.

1:12:48 The four pillars of biodefense
They broke biodefense into four layers: detection and surveillance (detecting pathogen sequences from environmental samples such as airport nasal swabs and wastewater systems), attribution (judging whether the source is natural, foreign, or engineered in some country's lab), countermeasures (making antivirals or antibacterials), and deterrence (at the government level). They focus on the first three. The core criticism is this: the existing biodefense community mainly relies on sequence matching — aligning sequences against databases of known pathogens. This cannot stop two things: new things that are not in the database, and designs that are deliberately obfuscated, that do not match in sequence space but have the same function.

1:25:15 You can't patch a human
The host points out the key difference between biosecurity and cybersecurity: in cybersecurity, a sufficiently strong model can in principle find every vulnerability and patch it, and as long as people keep updating, they are safe; but the genome is fixed, "you can't patch a human," so the defense surface is harder. Conversely there are two buffers: the intensity of motivation to launch an attack may be much lower, and the threshold from printing arbitrary DNA to building a successful virus — especially one that does not first kill the designer — is actually quite high.

item.title: The quantum scheme Google hid was overtaken by a group of amateur researchers
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-zeroknowledge-google-藏起来的量子方案-被一群业余研究者反超了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-zeroknowledge-google-藏起来的量子方案-被一群业余研究者反超了/
item.description: Google used a zero-knowledge proof to show it had found a more resource-efficient quantum attack, but wouldn't publish the circuit. Yukon turned the problem into an open competition where agents build on each other's submissions, and it ended up beating Google's result by more than 60%.
item.content:encoded:
Google used a zero-knowledge proof to show it had found a more resource-efficient quantum attack, but wouldn't publish the circuit. Yukon turned the problem into an open competition where agents build on each other's submissions, and it ended up beating Google's result by more than 60%.

High information density: it explains the mechanics of automated research competitions, verifier design, and several real breakthrough cases. Worth a listen for anyone following AI for science, ZK, and open innovation.

4:07 Google gives only the proof, not the circuit
Google published a paper claiming it had found a more resource-efficient quantum scheme than the previous state of the art, one that breaks the secp256k1 elliptic curve — the basis of Bitcoin and Ethereum public-key cryptography. But Google did not publish the scheme; instead it used a zero-knowledge proof to demonstrate that it really does possess such a scheme. Soubhik points out the consequence: if you want to prepare for Q-day, you have to know what schemes will appear, how to harden your systems, what the defences are; if you don't understand any of that, you are not prepared for Q-day. Not publishing the quantum circuit is the main consequence of this.

8:08 The competition isn't everyone for themselves, it's a relay
The way you take part in ecdsa.fail is not to do your work locally and then submit it. The platform backend runs the same verifier Google used; through a command-line interface you have your agent read the competition details and other people's submissions, then build directly on top of someone else's scheme. Soubhik says this is how research actually works: you build on each other's experience, not like an Olympic event where everyone submits independently. Anna says she had assumed it was PvP, with everyone finishing on their own machine and then submitting to compete; Soubhik confirms it isn't. This multi-user automated research framework produced enormous acceleration, because you don't have to rediscover everything yourself.

11:08 Three breakthroughs: externalising, mining, starting over
Soubhik sees three big breakthroughs. The first was externalising the environment and letting people outside the company take part — one team member who wasn't involved in the internal test spent about $5,000 on a codex subscription the day before the internal test and made a huge leap the lead engineer couldn't understand. The second was mining French's work, building on it, and surpassing Google's result within two weeks. After that the chart was almost a plateau for two months. The third happened in mid-August: Teddy, from Starkware, went back to the starting point of the competition, summarised all the tricks into a knowledge review, and then built from scratch rather than on other people's ideas, ultimately proposing the NSD ping-pong technique, which pushed the scheme from 49% better than Google to 57% better, and it has now passed 60%.

27:15 If the question isn't asked right, you can't run a competition
Soubhik says many problems are posed incorrectly, that is, badly formulated. He gives the example: ‘Build me a quantum computer’ — that problem is too big, we don't know what it is. But if you break it down, you find that the problem state of ecdsa.fail is one of its subproblems. You need to split the big problem into a series of well-formulated subtasks, then run automated research on each subtask. Another example is the proximity gap conjecture: EF committed a $1 million prize, but the original statement is binary — you either prove it or you don't — and it's hard to write a verifier for it. Later Alexander Hicks and Gako wrote a simple verifier for a specific instance of the conjecture, and that is what became the better.codes competition.

39:15 An algebraic geometer broke 64 bits in hours
better.codes has two bounds: the lower bound is the soundness bound, the upper bound is the attack bound. The lower bound had been stuck at the Johnson bound for years. On August 21 the competition was stuck at 63.99 bits, and 64 bits is the Johnson bound for this specific instance. Then there was no progress for 6 days, and the chart was a straight line. Until August 28, when the team contacted Bartosz from ECDSA — a Polish mathematician specialising in algebraic geometry, not a cryptographer at all, who had never heard of the problem. He came in and within a few hours pushed the result from 63.99 to 64.0101 bits, breaking the Johnson bound for the first time. The technique he used was some combination of algebraic geometry, because he was already using his own codex subscription to do algebraic geometry work, and he probably applied algebraic geometry methods to this problem.

41:15 One breakthrough set off a 30-year open problem
After Bartosz broke 64.01 bits, the whole circle blew up, with Ariel Gabizon, Kobi and others discussing it on Twitter. The story didn't end there: a few days later, some cryptographers had a bigger problem in coding theory that had been open for 30 years — proving a certain soundness bound. Within days three papers appeared claiming inspiration from the method used to break the Johnson bound. Soubhik says nobody could have predicted this; this is open innovation and collaborative research, and it still looks very early: people are starting to realise that problems they thought couldn't be solved for a long time can at least be pushed forward and improved.

45:18 Domain experts point the way for agents on GitHub
On the hish tiling problem, Yukon piloted a discussion-format feature. The whole process is in the CLI; you don't even need to think or prompt your agent. While doing research the agent searches for information in the hills and formulates strategies locally, and at the same time uploads discussions to a GitHub forum. Other agents read those discussions, and domain experts like Bartosz answer manually, and the agents then read those answers, so the domain expert is effectively guiding the automated research network. Soubhik says this is exactly what they want to achieve: a domain expert should be able to see how far the automated research network has got on his problem description, then use his best intuition to guide it and leave clues about what to explore.

52:20 Yukon wants to be an AI-native research institution
Soubhik says Yukon's vision is to grow into an AI-based research institution, imitating three features of traditional research institutions: research means building at a higher level on each other's ideas; credit must be given to the originators of ideas; and even failed ideas should be recognised, because one success may come out of a thousand failures. What AI changes is that the whole research lifecycle accelerates from months or years to days. They are implementing a partial credit system so people can give each other credit for ideas, including negative credit — failed ideas also get credit. They also want a system that helps you break a badly formulated problem into a series of well-formulated subproblems.

item.title: Russia Won't Invade NATO, but It Is Testing Whether NATO Will Fall Apart
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-goodfight-俄罗斯不会入侵北约-但正在测试它会不会散架/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-goodfight-俄罗斯不会入侵北约-但正在测试它会不会散架/
item.description: Russia has no capacity for a ground offensive; its real goal is to corrode NATO's political cohesion — using drones, parcel bombs and the grey zone to force the US to expose its divisions in a crisis.
item.content:encoded:
Russia has no capacity for a ground offensive; its real goal is to corrode NATO's political cohesion — using drones, parcel bombs and the grey zone to force the US to expose its divisions in a crisis.

The first half, on Russian hybrid warfare and NATO cohesion, is very dense; the second half on the Middle East is relatively diffuse, but the detail about Houthis using Claude to improve their missiles is worth hearing.

4:30 No ground-invasion risk, but hybrid-war escalation
Joshi says plainly: there is no risk of a Russian conventional ground offensive against NATO, this is not the kind of alarm it was in January 2022. The entire security apparatus of Estonia and Finland exists to detect exactly that kind of movement, and every port, naval base and forest route in western Russia is covered with intelligence and technical sensors. But another risk is rising: Russia's tolerance for hybrid operations below the Article V threshold is increasing. They have already used drones against Ukrainian cargo planes that might be bound for Ukraine, put explosives in DHL parcels in Leipzig, and sabotaged power plants and railways across Europe. The question is: would they actually fire missiles at Polish facilities? Joshi thinks Russia is still quite cautious and wants to avoid dragging NATO into a broader conflict, but that debate is not settled in Europe.

10:15 Poland sounds the loudest alarm, the Baltics say it's fine
The most alarming signal this week came from Poland. Tusk said intelligence indicated Russia might attack Poland and other NATO allies — not a conventional ground attack, but drones and missiles landing on NATO territory that Russia could portray as accidents. But Latvia's leadership, including the defence minister and the president, said there is no reason to panic and no elevated operational risk. Estonia also said it sees no risk of Russia aggressing in that way. Joshi says he has spoken to intelligence officials in multiple countries and there is no reason to fear a ground offensive. The disagreement is itself the information: Poland is raising the alarm, the Baltic states are cooling things down, and Russia is watching who believes whom.

14:20 Russia's real goal is to corrode NATO cohesion
Joshi points to Russia's political objective: not to conquer NATO territory or occupy Western Europe, but to weaken and break apart NATO's unity. The mechanism works like this: if a drone lands on Polish territory and blows up a warehouse, Russia says it was an accident, and then Trump says, "I spoke to Putin and he assured me it was an accident" — that lays the alliance's internal divisions bare. Under the Biden administration, Jake Sullivan would call the Russians and say that if this continues, you are risking us joining the war on Ukraine's side, and we will retaliate. But under the Trump administration, does Russia really believe Trump would step into a crisis the same way? So Russia has an opportunity not only to retaliate against attacks on Russia, but to test NATO's cohesion and its boundaries.

19:40 Trump on Ukraine: criticises in public, shares intelligence in private
Joshi says Trump's support for Ukraine is quite limited, far below Biden's. The US has effectively let weapons aid lapse; Ukraine desperately needs Patriot interceptor missiles, but because the US has used up so much in the Iran war, it has given Ukraine almost no interceptors recently. Diplomatically, the administration leans toward Russia and expects Ukraine to make concessions. But there are two exceptions: first, the new Graham bill, which the president has agreed to, would impose new sanctions on Russian entities and force Trump to levy tariffs on countries that buy Russian oil and do not reduce their purchases — in effect China and India, and possibly Central European countries. Second, Trump is quietly, not publicly, providing intelligence to Ukraine to help it strike Russian energy facilities. That is the strange reversal: Trump criticises Ukraine overall, but secret assistance is still happening.

26:10 The Strait of Hormuz is still half-closed
The Trump administration insists this is not a war; Trump calls it an "excursion." But the Strait of Hormuz remains largely closed, with oil traffic far below pre-war levels. There is no deal with Iran, no resolution. There are no formal limits on Iran's nuclear programme and no formal commitment to reopen Hormuz. Trump faces the midterms in a month and desperately needs to avoid a sharp escalation of the war that would send oil prices soaring. But politically he cannot make the concessions to Iran needed for a deal, because that would be too humiliating, too obviously equivalent to defeat, and would look extremely bad before the election. So it is a stalemate: Iran has considerable control over the strait, with occasional clashes — the US bombs Iranian coastal missile bases, Iran strikes tankers trying to pass through Hormuz.

31:45 Houthis used Claude to improve ballistic missiles
Joshi tells a shocking detail: when Anthropic published its report on harmful uses of Claude, one of the examples was Houthis using Claude to improve their ballistic missile programme. This group, widely seen as technologically primitive, is using the most advanced AI on Earth to improve the guidance systems of the ballistic missiles they fire at Middle East shipping. Mounk adds that being able — at least until being cut off — to access the most advanced American technology to strike America and America's allies is itself a fascinating story. This connects the Ukraine and Russia discussion with the Houthi discussion: in modern war, defensive capability dominates on the ground, but offensive capability dominates in the air.

38:20 Perception is the primary problem on the battlefield
Joshi offers a unified framework to explain why ground defence dominates while air strikes remain effective: it is all about perception. To hit something, you first need to perceive it — find it on the battlefield, then fire at it. That is much harder than it sounds. Perception is the primary problem on the battlefield; actually firing is secondary. On the Ukrainian front line, this is a sensor-saturated environment: small drones everywhere, thermal cameras detecting movement at night, radar penetrating foliage, satellites targeting the area. Anything that moves gets hit; it is a kill zone. But you cannot perceive everywhere equally easily. Drones can see ten kilometres behind the battlefield, but fifty kilometres back, satellite coverage is patchy. It is like the fog of war in a real-time strategy game — you send units out and the fog lifts, but where you have not been remains fog. That is why Iran can still launch ballistic missiles, and why Houthis can fire missiles from the mountains of Yemen into the Red Sea.

item.title: US Debt Tops $40 Trillion: Even the Doves Are Turning Hawkish
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-planetmoney-美国债务破-40-万亿-连鸽派都改口当鹰派了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-planetmoney-美国债务破-40-万亿-连鸽派都改口当鹰派了/
item.description: The 2010 paper claiming growth halves once debt exceeds 90% of GDP was used by politicians as a red line for over a decade; now even the dove economist who argued for bold spending calls herself a hawk, but no one can say where that line is.
item.content:encoded:
The 2010 paper claiming growth halves once debt exceeds 90% of GDP was used by politicians as a red line for over a decade; now even the dove economist who argued for bold spending calls herself a hawk, but no one can say where that line is.

Medium information density, but the second half's reversal of positions and the interest rate data are worth it. For understanding how the US debt debate evolved from 2010 to today, this episode is a clear recap.

2:05 The real fuse on the debt snowball is interest
The textbook worry isn't the debt itself, but that interest costs feed on themselves: pay more interest, the deficit grows; a bigger deficit pushes debt higher; next period's interest is even bigger, and so on compounding worse and worse. The other path is investors losing their appetite for Treasuries, forcing the government to keep raising rates to attract buyers, making the snowball roll faster. Neither of these feared outcomes happened after the financial crisis, and in hindsight the people who argued the government should spend more were on the right side of history — Karen Dynan even thinks it should have spent more and the recession could have been shorter.

8:21 The 90% line was read into the paper
The 2010 six-page paper by Reinhart and Rogoff, "Growth in a Time of Debt," studied decades of debt data from 20 advanced economies and concluded that when debt reaches 90% of GDP, growth is only half its normal level. But what the paper actually did was sort countries into four buckets — low, medium, high, and very high — with the very high bucket containing countries with debt far above 90%, and technically it said that this bucket, on average and over long periods, was associated with lower growth. Politicians and the media read it as a red line: "cross 90% and the economy crashes." The paper never said that.

11:28 An Excel error ignited the austerity fight
The debate the paper sparked raged in blogs and newspapers, with calls for austerity and belt-tightening on one side and warnings not to kill the recovery and stop spending now on the other. Later, more debt-friendly economists pointed out a major error in the Excel spreadsheet Reinhart and Rogoff used, and the paper's final sentence said that since their finding was wrong, the austerity agendas in Europe and the US should be reassessed. Correcting the error weakened the claim everyone had seized on, but didn't overturn it — the updated paper still showed high debt generally associated with slower growth, just less steeply.

13:41 Low growth can also cause high debt
High debt being correlated with low growth doesn't mean high debt causes low growth. Andrea Presbitero points out the causality could run the other way: when the economy underperforms, policymakers want to stimulate it, which means public consumption and public investment, and one way to pay for that is borrowing — borrowing pushes debt up, so you see low growth and high debt in the data at the same time. He and his coauthors ultimately reached the same conclusion as most: based on the empirical evidence, there's no definitive answer, and causality may run both ways. Moreover, the debt threshold varies by country — it could be 90%, 45%, or 100% — and depends on who the creditors are, whether they're domestic or foreign investors, and whether the debt is short-term or long-term.

17:50 Zero rates shelved the whole issue
What makes high debt destructive isn't the debt itself but the interest paid on it. After the financial crisis, global rates fell to near zero and stayed there for years, so many macroeconomists thought maybe there was no need to worry much about debt, and attention drifted away from the topic. Then the world changed twice: the pandemic and the spending that followed pushed debt even higher, and more importantly, rates rose again. Today the cost of holding a lot of debt is much higher for the US and other countries than five or six years ago, and the shelved question is relevant again.

19:57 Rogoff says 91% and you're doomed is a misreading
Ken Rogoff is still annoyed by how the paper was interpreted. He says 90% was just their highest bucket, and they never said that at 91% you suddenly go to hell — that's like a 55 mph speed limit and you drive 56, so you'll crash the next minute. He thinks that interpretation was used and distorted polemically. But he also stresses that you can't therefore say there's no threshold and any level of debt is fine — that's crazy too. His basic intuition hasn't changed: constantly leveraging up is playing with fire, and the US trajectory needs adjusting, not just debt but also Social Security and Medicare.

25:22 The dove who argued for spending has flipped
Two years later, debt has grown by more than $4 trillion, the large tax cuts Congress passed in 2025 further reduced revenue, and interest alone costs over $1 trillion a year, a record. Karen Dynan, who once thought spending was worth the risk, now says, "I'm a debt hawk now," because changes in financial markets, especially Treasury borrowing rates, make her think this is trickier than she thought two years ago. She describes it as walking on ice and comforting yourself that it hasn't cracked yet. Last week the 10-year Treasury rate hit its highest level since before the Great Recession, and the CBO projects debt will exceed 120% of GDP by 2036, higher than at any point in US history including World War II.

28:32 Rogoff puts the odds of a big problem above 50%
Rogoff thinks the biggest misconception is believing rates will stay low forever, and that if they're high for a while, it's just a nightmare that will pass. He says he thinks the probability of something very serious happening is greater than 50% — not the end of the world, a debt crisis isn't the end of the world, but something very significant will happen and we're not prepared. He also says we need to reflect on how wrong everyone was and for how long, because that belief hasn't disappeared — mainstream opinion leaders think basically the same now as they did then. As for the red line, neither economist can draw it, but both agree the solution is spending cuts, tax increases, or both, and that looks impossible to push through.

item.title: Silicon Valley Makes Too Much Money, and That's Why California's Government Has No Reason to Get Better
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-allin-硅谷太赚钱-反而让加州政府没有变好的动力/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-allin-硅谷太赚钱-反而让加州政府没有变好的动力/
item.description: California has been a one-party state for 16 years — not because voters want big government, but because Silicon Valley's tax payments are so generous that the government doesn't need to survive on results. Gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton says the price is the highest poverty rate, unemployment rate and cost of living in the country.
item.content:encoded:
California has been a one-party state for 16 years — not because voters want big government, but because Silicon Valley's tax payments are so generous that the government doesn't need to survive on results. Gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton says the price is the highest poverty rate, unemployment rate and cost of living in the country.

What's worth listening for is two checkable causal chains: how Sacramento's bill assembly line piles up 420,000 regulations, and how Silicon Valley's tax revenue removes the government's need to improve.

5:04 The rules aren't written, they're piled up every year
Hilton gives a countable form to the consequences of one-party rule: Sacramento passed 1,118 bills last year, and when he printed them out, the stack was twice his height. "Nobody's reading this" — do you think Gavin Newsom reads them before signing? The result is that California has accumulated more than 420,000 regulations, and he promises to cut that below 200,000 within his first term. Who are the bills written for? He says for the narrow interest groups that control the process: unions, plaintiff's attorneys, and the people who donate to politicians. That's why California is the highest litigation-risk place in the country, and starting a company in California carries a 90% chance of ending up in court. Structurally, over those 16 years Democrats took every one of the eight statewide elected offices, a two-thirds majority in the state legislature, every major county and major city, and a 6-to-1 majority on the state Supreme Court.

13:08 The key is that 26% of undecided voters
What he offers isn't a "Republicans flip it" story but an arithmetic problem: his internal poll at the start of the campaign was 33% firmly for him, 41% firmly for Becerra, 26% undecided. That 26% is the key — mostly people who have voted Democratic but aren't die-hards, overwhelmingly non-college-educated working people who are financially maxed out, and their top concern is the cost of living. So the platform is all priceable line items: cancel high-speed rail, cut the government payroll by 10%, stop funding the nonprofits that make homelessness worse, and that adds up to "the first $150,000 free of state income tax"; gas goes from $6 toward $3, because the low carbon fuel standard and cap and invest add roughly 150 dollars to the price of gas, and cap and invest money is flowing to high-speed rail; vehicle registration fees capped at 73 dollars, by abolishing the DMV. The polling gap has narrowed from 30 points on primary night to 8 points recently.

19:14 Silicon Valley's money removes the pressure to perform
This is the most counterintuitive stretch of the whole piece. One host cites Peter Thiel's observation from years ago: Silicon Valley is like a resource curse for California — it generates so much wealth and tax revenue that the place doesn't need a good government, and that's also why one-party rule persists. Hilton adds the evidence: before the primary, Becerra was asked on CNN what policies he'd change given homelessness, the highest poverty rate, the highest unemployment rate, and a terrible cost of living, and his answer was that this is the world's fourth-largest economy, people still love coming to Disneyland and the beaches, so things must be heading in the right direction. Hilton's rebuttal is that the fourth-largest-economy figure includes the size of the government itself — which doubled in a decade — while net private-sector job creation in California since the pandemic has been essentially zero.

23:19 What works is the content, not the AI
Spencer Pratt is running for mayor of Los Angeles as an independent and got a huge amount of free media off a batch of AI-generated videos. He breaks down the mechanism himself: what actually worked was what the videos said — he went on every platform and just told the truth as he knows it, and then creative people across the country threw ideas into this "machine." "I don't think it's the AI that worked, it's just one piece of a lot of puzzle pieces." He thinks there's evidence for this: most of the people who voted for him are Democrats. He also claims that if the 200,000 registered Republicans in Los Angeles had actually turned out to vote, he would have won.

27:21 Taxpayers are paying for needles handed out in the park
Hilton and Spencer together describe MacArthur Park: last Tuesday at 10:30 in the morning, sunny in downtown Los Angeles, and in every direction you look people are smoking crack, injecting drugs, some bent over from fentanyl. The reason is that four nonprofits show up every day to hand out crack pipes, needles and drug supplies, and the money comes from taxpayers. Spencer adds the follow-up: one of the needle distributors was found to be selling drugs at the same time. Hilton stresses that this isn't a case of nobody being in charge — Los Angeles has a new DA cracking down on drugs and crime, and there are federal prosecutors going after gangs and cartels — but the scene in the park is the same every Tuesday.

29:22 Do the right thing and you're punished, do the wrong thing and you're rewarded
A Latino couple in South Los Angeles ran a shoe store for 14 years, the shop was spotless, and they paid taxes, licenses, electricity, and permits that got more expensive every year, without fail. They asked Hilton to step outside and look at the sidewalk two blocks away: it was entirely vendors selling shoes, clothing and T-shirts who pay no taxes, no electricity, no rent, no license. That's why the couple is closing. When did it start? In the last six or seven years — in 2018 Sacramento passed a bill legalizing street vending statewide, and cities and counties have no authority over it. His conclusion: here doing the right thing is punished and doing the wrong thing is rewarded, the whole thing is upside down. Spencer adds the numbers: 50,000 food vendors, a permit costs just 21 dollars, yet the city council allocated 500,000 dollars to buy them carts, while the unbuilt Palisades reservoir cover only needed 200,000 dollars.

42:32 Ballot collection is legal, so it can't be audited
Spencer's claim is: it's not fake ballots, it's ballot harvesting, which California law allows. The mechanism has three steps: a witness signature can be a smiley face or an X; the same witness can witness 43,000 ballots, and there's no verification allowed; and once ballots reach the counting center they're separated from the envelopes, the signatures stay on the envelopes, and the chain of custody is broken — so even if you know who these people are, you can't audit it, and a recount just recounts the same batch of ballots. The rebuttal from the other side: voter fraud is a felony and is prosecuted regularly; after Trump lost last time he filed 60 lawsuits of this kind and lost all of them. Asked directly whether he believes he lost because of fraud, Spencer's answer is "without evidence I'd say no," and he lists the 200,000 registered Republicans who didn't vote as one of the reasons.

47:35 The empty reservoir and the reconstruction lawsuit
Spencer's house, his parents' house and his neighbors' houses all burned. Reconstruction is stuck on two things. First, that empty reservoir is still empty, even the one across from his house that he was sure would never burn is empty, and what's supplying Palisades now is a hose run all the way from Tanga through regrown dry brush. Second, they're pursuing a mass tort suit with 10,000 victims, against Gavin Newsom's state parks, the city, and the city's water and power department. His chain of allegations: on New Year's Eve there was an 8-acre fire in Pacific Palisades, state parks should have monitored it per the manual but didn't, letting embers smolder into the known high-wind weather of January 6 and 7; firefighter whistleblowers told him there were visibly smoldering coals on the hillside, and state parks employees produced photos in testimony showing the hillside smoking.

item.title: Individual productivity tripled, but company delivery only went from 20 days to 17
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-lightstar-个人提效三倍-公司交付只从20天缩到17天/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-lightstar-个人提效三倍-公司交付只从20天缩到17天/
item.description: AI armed everyone, but the organization didn't get faster — because the weakest link isn't people, it's process. The real dividing line is whether you can transform process and organization, not whether you hand out tokens to employees.
item.content:encoded:
AI armed everyone, but the organization didn't get faster — because the weakest link isn't people, it's process. The real dividing line is whether you can transform process and organization, not whether you hand out tokens to employees.

A frontline CEO talks about building his own CEO AI, canceling weekly meetings, and using token consumption to identify elite performers — the mechanisms and numbers are concrete, and the decision hub section in the second half is the most valuable.

16:07 Individual productivity tripled, delivery only sped up three days
NetEase did a count last year: a software requirement, from the product manager receiving it and producing a design doc to the feature going live, averaged 20 working days. After AI coding crossed the inflection point, many engineers doubled or even tripled to quintupled their personal efficiency, some tenfold. But for features of the same scope, the whole process only shrank from 20 days to 17. The reason is that a team completing a complex task is like a barrel: of 20 staves, 10 are engineers, 3 are product, 3 are testing. The engineer and product manager staves shot up fast, but some staves aren't people — they're process — and they didn't improve at all. So AI adoption has to clear three hurdles: cognition, landing on individual short-range tasks, and transforming process and organization. The third is the hardest.

20:11 Cancel the weekly meeting: AI syncs information, people only solve problems
Ruan Liang asked friends who run companies whether they still hold weekly meetings; 99% said yes. Weekly meetings usually serve three purposes: sync information, discover problems and opportunities, and make decisions. It used to be 2.5 hours a week, but the time spent on this meeting could be ten times 2.5 hours — every department prepares materials layer by layer, and the information sync itself isn't done well, because no one listens attentively the whole time and may miss a sentence relevant to them. After the reform: the general manager and management agree on what information is needed, everyone fills in a template and stores it in the knowledge base, AI scans and integrates it into a focused, interactive HTML report where people can leave comments and follow-up questions; an AI agent produces a list of problems and opportunities in advance, which human brains confirm and supplement; solving problems and making decisions move to dedicated meetings.

28:20 SaaS isn't dead, but ordinary SaaS will die
Ruan Liang doesn't think SaaS is dead: SaaS is essentially Service, and Service always exists, it just changes form — AI as a Service and Agent as a Service are themselves software. But ordinary SaaS may really die, while genuinely good SaaS that has entered a company's critical processes will only get better, because it becomes internal infrastructure. In the past, humans used software, limited by time and energy; in the future, a large number of Agents will call databases, APIs, security APIs, review APIs, HR APIs, CRM APIs — call volume will far exceed the number and actions of humans, will grow enormously, and the more it's called the more entrenched it becomes. The premise is that this Service itself is critical enough inside the company.

32:21 Distill top salespeople into skills and distribute them to everyone
Bosses have two headaches: the sales team has only one or two strong performers and the rest are mediocre; or a salesperson is too strong and what if they leave. There used to be no solution, but now you can distill or extract a good salesperson's moves, scripts, and behaviors into skills. Two uses: distribute them to other salespeople to use directly; and have AI turn elite salespeople into teachers to train ordinary salespeople. What training should distill isn't the salesperson, it's the customer — take the customer interaction data a salesperson has touched, such as calls, WeChat, emails, and let AI simulate various customers to train salespeople. Online sales is purely digital and on record; for offline sales, recommend or even require a recording card — after a visit, while memory is fresh, record a two-to-three-minute voice note, because salespeople dislike CRM (they think CRM is for managing them), but they don't mind a recording card, because it's also useful for their own customer review.

44:31 Fewer middle managers, strong individuals lead Agent legions back to the front line
Ruan Liang judges that middle managers will become fewer, but not necessarily be eliminated — rather, they'll go to the front line, and the front line can also lead a bunch of agents. Middle managers performing management duties will become fewer, and elite people with strong skills will become more numerous. He gives the example of an engineering team: previously socialized division of labor split software development ever finer — frontend, backend, algorithm, test engineers; in the last half year it has clearly reverted to full-stack, everyone becoming full-end engineers. In the future the organization will look more and more like a distributed structure, with countless strong engineers, a mother peak commanding some engineers, and countless agents fighting a battle. He imagines a future interview negotiation scenario: the candidate says I'm not one person, I bring an AI team, a summary of all my past experience and skills, and the premium the company pays might be some kind of OPC.

50:35 AI value formula: quality times time saved
Ruan Liang gives a formula referencing a paper: AI's value = the quality of AI completing the task (as a ratio of human quality) × time saved × the company's economic value per unit time. For example, a human makes a cup of coffee at eight out of ten, AI also makes it at eight out of ten, so the quality coefficient is 1; a human takes 20 minutes, AI takes only 10 seconds, saving 14 minutes 50 seconds; multiply by the company's economic value per unit time and you can calculate ROI. Prioritize four types of things for AI to do: time-consuming, high-frequency, unavoidable, and where different people produce roughly the same result. Once calculated, you can immediately decide whether to use AI. He also suggests first using the most expensive AI (Cloud, GPT) to prove the thing can be done, solidify the process, then switch to cheaper ones — if the most expensive can do it, within two months the cheap ones can too.

59:40 Token consumption leads by a landslide, output also leads by a landslide
NetEase started a points system in 2024, trying to quantify engineers' work tasks into points with work value. By the AI era they found a type of person whose token consumption is astonishing, and whose work output and work value are also astonishing, forming a statistical pattern: people whose token consumption leads by a landslide are most likely building systems for themselves, saving their own work time and increasing thinking time, so their work quality and work results also lead by a landslide. Many bosses worry about waste from AI abuse; Ruan Liang's hot take is that truly excellent or elite people won't waste — the company has audits but doesn't tell colleagues, and through statistics they found elite colleagues don't waste. He also says small companies are more likely to fully embrace AI, because there are fewer organizational relationships, the boss uses it first, hierarchy is shallow, and the chain is short.

1:11:50 The core of a decision hub is decision history, not the model
Building an AI decision hub essentially requires a high-quality knowledge base, and what really matters is the historical decision processes and decision bases. This year NetEase preserved decisions that happened historically, incorporated them into the knowledge base, combined the two types of knowledge to train an agent or skill, then fed back the original several hundred cases for the agent to judge, achieving over 90% accuracy. Ruan Liang also mentions that Bridgewater gave researchers and analysts agents it built itself, precipitating decision processes and decision history into a decision knowledge base; what Bridgewater did better was making the agent a learnable, evolvable part — after a person adjusts it, the confirmed adjustment action enters the next round of reinforcement, keeping pace with the times, equivalent to human-machine collaborative self-evolution.

item.title: Mooncakes sell for only two months a year, yet they've become a 28.2 billion yuan business
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-beiwanglu-月饼一年只卖两个月-却做成了282亿的生意/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-beiwanglu-月饼一年只卖两个月-却做成了282亿的生意/
item.description: Being bound to Mid-Autumn Festival actually traps mooncakes' selling window, but the 28.2 billion yuan scale comes from gifting scenarios and flexible custom production lines, not from flavor innovation.
item.content:encoded:
Being bound to Mid-Autumn Festival actually traps mooncakes' selling window, but the 28.2 billion yuan scale comes from gifting scenarios and flexible custom production lines, not from flavor innovation.

Worth listening for food industry practitioners and anyone wanting to understand the holiday consumption business, but information density is low, with much of the runtime spent on explaining regional styles and flavors, and the business mechanics concentrated in the middle-to-late sections.

6:06 Zongzi can sell year-round, mooncakes cannot
Zongzi is tied to Dragon Boat Festival, but once vacuum-sealed for long shelf life it can sell all year round, and Wufangzhai (五芳斋) even opened restaurants to put zongzi into everyday scenarios. Mooncakes' problem is not that the craft can't achieve long shelf life, but that they are defined as ‘traditional festival pastries mainly eaten during Mid-Autumn Festival’, and the national standard GB19855 writes the season directly into the definition. So for the same kind of festival food, zongzi can decouple from the holiday through shelf life and channels, while mooncakes cannot.

12:12 The national standard draws hard lines for fillings
Lotus seed paste mooncakes must contain no less than 60% lotus seeds, fruit mooncakes must contain no less than 25% fruit products, and five-kernel mooncakes must use the five kernels: walnut, almond, olive kernel, melon seed, and sesame. The purpose of this line is to push up ingredient costs and prevent passing off cheap candied winter melon, green and red shreds, and inferior nuts as the real thing. For consumers, reading the order of ingredients on the label is enough to judge how much is actually used.

26:30 Why custard lava mooncakes are made so small
Custard lava mooncakes are small not out of stinginess, but because of structure. The outside is flaky pastry, the middle is a custard layer, and the innermost is the lava layer, with the custard layer serving to block moisture. Production requires two rounds of baking to keep the lava semi-solid, and the melting point of the lava must be designed — solid during transport, becoming flowing liquid only after a few seconds in the microwave. If heated too much, the lava is absorbed dry by the pastry and it reverts to an ordinary custard mooncake.

37:34 Everything can be a mooncake has five prerequisites
Not everything can be stuffed into a mooncake. First is water content — hot and sour soup mooncakes can't be made because there's too much water to wrap; second is safety — meat, egg, and dairy are also favored by microorganisms, so processing temperature and sterilization processes must be repeatedly tested; third is particle size — too large and the pastry can't hold it, too fine and you can't taste it; fourth is flavor retention after high-temperature baking — some aromas disappear once baked; fifth is whether the cost can be handled. So long-term stable flavors are confirmed by generation after generation.

44:40 Choosing an OEM factory isn't about picking the biggest
When big brands make branded mooncakes through OEM, there's a common misconception: you must choose the best OEM factory in the country. But the top OEM factory's production scale actually doesn't match yours. Indicators you can screen for include registered capital, tax payment records, number of employees with social insurance contributions, and accumulated days of safe production. Also, the nine major regional styles correspond to different factories — you can't ask Guangzhou Restaurant (广州酒家) to produce Shanxi egg-skin mooncakes, they don't have that capability or production line.

48:44 Flexible production lines can take orders of a few hundred boxes
Mooncake production is semi-automated and semi-manual — wrapping and forming machines can do the work, but brushing egg wash, pressing patterns, and stamping require human hands, which actually makes it favorable for OEM and customization. Flexible factories can go as small as a few hundred boxes, and can do thousands or tens of thousands of boxes. If a company has only 50 employees, they can directly use the factory's existing mooncakes and only need to design the paper box. This small-batch quick-response capability is the core of why mooncakes can do corporate custom business.

51:47 The 28.2 billion yuan scale is propped up by gifting
In 2025 China's mooncake output was 518,000 tons, with sales of 28.2 billion RMB, both down from the previous year. At 80 grams each that's about 6.4 billion pieces, at 100 grams about 5.18 billion pieces, and across a population of 1.4 billion that's an average of three to four pieces per person. For comparison, Dragon Boat Festival zongzi annual sales are about 10 to 11 billion, and instant noodles about 68 to 120 billion. Mooncakes selling for only two months a year can reach 28.2 billion, and the core is the gifting attribute — brands prepare large amounts of PR gifts at the two nodes of Chinese New Year and Mid-Autumn Festival, and zongzi's gifting attribute is far weaker than mooncakes'.

58:55 499 yuan is a number forced out by the regulatory line
In 2022 the National Development and Reform Commission and three other departments jointly issued an announcement implementing key supervision over boxed mooncakes priced above 500 yuan per unit. So the highest price on the market is 499. The calculation logic is: a box of mooncakes costs about 70 yuan per box, and adding channel deductions and allocated expenses, it's impossible to exceed 500. In better economic times there were sky-high mooncakes with very expensive tea or liquor inside, even wooden gift boxes, with both cost and price very high.

item.title: AI for Science Is Stuck on the Last 0.001 Points, Not on Compute
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-latentspace-ai-做科学卡在最后-0-001-分-不是卡在算力/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-latentspace-ai-做科学卡在最后-0-001-分-不是卡在算力/
item.description: ERA can churn out thousands of candidate notebooks, but it can't close the gap on the last 30 places — because the inner loop is a machine, and the outer loop still needs a human to say ‘you got this paper wrong’.
item.content:encoded:
ERA can churn out thousands of candidate notebooks, but it can't close the gap on the last 30 places — because the inner loop is a machine, and the outer loop still needs a human to say ‘you got this paper wrong’.

High information density, but it takes a little patience: the first half covers ERA's mechanics, the second half covers contrails, wildfires and quantum computing, all first-hand detail.

9:24 ERA's input is a chat, its output is a scored notebook
ERA's product form isn't having people write config files — you just start chatting. Because mapping a scientific problem onto a scorable task is itself non-obvious, Michael Brenner wrote a dedicated agent to conversationally help you define which score to optimize. When the conversation ends, a Python notebook is generated underneath, containing a function that produces a score, and then the system starts mutating that notebook in a ‘clever way’, continually proposing new code to push the score higher.

10:24 It doesn't always pick the best candidate
ERA runs Monte Carlo Tree Search internally, holding hundreds or thousands of notebook candidates at once in a tree-shaped pool. Selection uses the upper confidence bound from reinforcement learning: it estimates the 95th percentile outcome of a mutation and picks the one with the highest optimistic upper bound. So it isn't always greedily choosing the currently best-performing notebook — sometimes it picks the fifth best, in order to explore more efficiently. It has also tried splicing the ideas of two candidates together to generate a third.

18:38 Evolutionary coding was stuck for decades because random mutation is useless
Platt says evolutionary coding goes back to the 1970s — mutating Lisp code and so on — but it never took off, because random mutation in code space is basically worthless: just like DNA, the vast majority of mutations are harmful. ERA works because the inner loop is itself an AI that knows which direction to try, which amounts to having a meaningful gradient underneath. The price is that it also overfits, and it also goes off the rails in ‘genie wish’ fashion.

22:44 Predictive models and descriptive models are two different things
John Platt splits scientific modeling into two kinds: a predictive model just seeks the lowest error rate on some dataset; a descriptive model is what science actually wants, because it contains some description of reality inside it, and so it can extrapolate. His example is Newton: an apple falling can be fit, but gravity isn't about apples — take a model that only fits apples and ask it about planets, and it has no planetary data, so it knows nothing. He admits the line is blurry, because the scientist themself also constrains the model with a pile of known facts and intuitions.

31:59 This is a power tool, and it will cut your fingers off
Faced with multiple hypothesis testing and overfitting, Platt's answer isn't a new method but a harsher version of an old one: because ERA is a power tool, you have to be stricter than before, with a holdout buried so deep you never look at it yourself. He states plainly that no system yet discovers entirely new physics or entirely new science, and that scientists are still responsible for judging whether a conclusion is descriptive.

39:18 AI is stuck on the last 0.001 points
Ira pushed the score very close, but it didn't close the gap on roughly the last 30 places, because nobody goes and scrapes out that final 0.001. This exposes the system's real structure: the inner layer is a machine running for hours to produce candidates, and the outer layer is a human making judgments like ‘you got this paper wrong’. Platt compares it to a graduate student who never sleeps and is extremely eager — you tell it a direction, it goes and tries, but when it gets stuck a human has to change the approach.

48:08 The counterfactual model stalled the team for two years
To judge which contrail to avoid, you need to know how much warming it actually causes, and that's a counterfactual problem: you can't enter the universe where the contrail doesn't exist. The team produced a counterfactual model that worked for outgoing longwave radiation, but they could never build one for the reflected-sunlight part, and it stalled them for two years. They even self-tested with a dataset of artificially injected contrails, and their own attempt couldn't pass their own test. In the end ERA found a simple model that searches over all confounders, passed the test, and cracked the problem.

1:24:27 A wildfire is best put out before it's room-sized
Google has a crisis resilience effort, and one project in it is Firesat: a wildfire is extremely easy to extinguish when it's only as big as ‘this room’, and once it reaches an acre it's far harder, while the growth from room-sized to an acre may be exponential. The plan is a low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation using mid-wave IR detection (which corresponds to blackbody radiation, exactly the temperature of fire); roughly 50 to 80 satellites could cover the globe, spot a fire about 5 meters across, and raise an alarm within 15 to 20 minutes. The partner is the nonprofit Earth Fire Alliance, the satellites are built by Muon Space, and one prototype has already launched.

item.title: Trump Invites Xi to a Show. What Did the US Get in Return?
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-特朗普请习近平看戏-美国换到了什么实质东西/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-特朗普请习近平看戏-美国换到了什么实质东西/
item.description: This state visit has almost no substantive agenda — it is pure symbolism and optics. The question is not whether something goes wrong, but what the US got in exchange for the symbolism. So far: nothing.
item.content:encoded:
This state visit has almost no substantive agenda — it is pure symbolism and optics. The question is not whether something goes wrong, but what the US got in exchange for the symbolism. So far: nothing.

The first half covers the summit and US-China relations; the middle and later sections on China after Xi and fifty years since Mao's death are denser and more worth hearing.

6:06 This visit has no substantive agenda at all
Gewirtz's judgment is that this state visit has "there is not a very deep substantive agenda at all." Trump invited Xi mainly because he wants to put on a show, wants the pomp and the cameras, and wants to push topics like the Iran war out of the news. For Beijing, that actually makes them less nervous — because if it were a more confrontational meeting, they would be more anxious. But Gewirtz flags two things: Trump himself is extremely unpredictable, and Beijing has internalized that; and Beijing watches the chaos in Washington and sees the American president himself often in a position they would never want Xi to be in — going to the wrong place, being photographed in unflattering images, being pressed by reporters. So the real question is not whether someone deliberately sets a trap, but whether they slip into the scenario they are trying hardest to avoid.

9:25 Symbolism for substance: where is the trade
Gewirtz characterizes this visit as "we are in a space of symbolism and optics." He says that in US-China relations, trading symbolism for substance is itself a reasonable play: give Beijing the pomp and cameras it craves, and get back something concretely useful to Americans and American interests. That was the model for US relations with the Soviets during the Cold War and after — the US gave symbolism, legitimacy and that handshake photo, and got a step back from the other side on third-world countries or nuclear issues. But the problem this time is that the Trump administration does not even seem to have tried to design a set of "deliverables." Gewirtz says "it doesn't even seem like they're trying." So what to watch is not where something goes wrong, but "where is the trade happening."

11:37 The direction of concessions has been flipped entirely
Gewirtz points to a counterintuitive dynamic: concessions the US might once have given China are now flipped into "gifts" China gives the US. Pomp and cameras were what Beijing wanted, but in Washington they are treated as Xi's visit being a concession to the US. The same flip happens on advanced semiconductors: the US used to not sell these things, and opening up products like the H200 would have been a huge concession; now, if Beijing agrees to buy, many in Washington would see it as Beijing conceding to Trump. Gewirtz says this flip keeps recurring, and the reason it matters is not to score points for the administration, but that it reflects what happens in superpower competition when the power gap narrows — very small differences, interpersonal dynamics, can produce much larger displacements in the overall strategic picture.

12:39 US-China relations are also K-shaped, held up by the upper leg
Gewirtz uses the "K-shape" to talk about US-China relations: one upward leg is the leader-level channel — dense exchanges of visits, friendship, cameras; one downward leg is the competitive reality and the actions some parts of both governments keep taking. The system is currently held up by the upward leg, but it is very fragile. He stresses the metaphor is not just a parallel analogy: saying "truce" or "detente" sounds too static, like a state already reached, but US-China relations are actually quite dynamic, quite unstable, moving in two directions at once. He applies the same K-shaped logic to China's economy — manufacturing and AI are flying, real estate and consumer demand are struggling, the upward leg is pulling the whole system forward, and the question is whether the system can hold as the K widens.

22:03 The bipartisan consensus on China policy has shattered
Gewirtz argues that Trump changed the tone of America's China discussion in the 2016 election and became the symbol and standard-bearer of that turn; but now, after helping create that turn, he has helped destroy or reshape it. He cites David Feith's article in the Reagan Institute on "a new cold war in an age of doubt" — that great rethink on China was not as great as many assumed. Gewirtz's conclusion: if the political dynamics are more complicated than imagined and the bipartisan consensus some people talk about does not exist, then this is a moment of "incredible fluidity." He says he has no confidence in the direction of either Democratic or Republican China policy in the medium term, and Beijing has no confidence either.

31:24 Chinese officials cannot talk about risks they have no solution for
Gewirtz offers a different read on how the US should interpret Chen Yixin's article. On the surface, Americans are panicking about existential risk and China is panicking about regime security, and that is correct. But he says: heads of American AI model companies can talk at length about risks they have no solution for, and all of them do; China's minister of state security cannot. In China, when you point out a risk in public, you are simultaneously saying "we the Communist Party see it, we will handle it, we have a solution." So the real question is: should we treat what we can see from Beijing as everything, or acknowledge that there is more in the system that we cannot see. He gives an example from 25 years ago — when Americans predicted the internet would cause regime change in China, Clinton said that was like nailing Jell-O to the wall, and Beijing did nail the Jell-O to the wall, namely the firewall.

35:37 Beijing has not decided how to regulate open models
Gewirtz says that around Xi's speech and Chen Yixin's article, the outside world has already been through several cycles of excitement and interpretation, but Beijing has still not given the single most important thing: how it plans to regulate open-weight models spreading globally — models that carry both risk and strategic benefit for Beijing. He calls this "the trillion dollar question." Both speeches can be read as pointing in some direction, but the decision has not been made. His guess is that this is because Beijing itself has not decided, because things are changing too fast and the trade-offs are too large. He contrasts the Trump administration: it did not make a decision until Mythos came out, and then made another when Fable came out.

41:55 What to prepare for is not China's decline but Xi's decline
Gewirtz says that a few years ago the "peak China" debate asked whether to start preparing for China's decline, and now most people think China's economy is at least for the moment on a relatively sustainable path. But he thinks the real question is not that, but "do we need to prepare for Xi Jinping's decline" — because people die, and modern Chinese history tells us that leaders in power for a long time change with age, certain obsessions become more prominent, behavior changes. By "prepare" he does not mean the departure itself, but acknowledging uncertainty: the outside world has treated Xi's tenure as fairly predictable, because since taking power in 2012 and 2013 he laid out a set of goals and largely pursued them. But he stresses the change could absolutely be worse for the US — "That doesn't mean he's going to mellow."

item.title: Canada Wants Into the EU: This Is a Permanent Breakup With America, Not a Wait for Trump to Leave
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-wsjournal-加拿大想加入欧盟-这是对美国的永久分手-不是等特朗普下台/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-wsjournal-加拿大想加入欧盟-这是对美国的永久分手-不是等特朗普下台/
item.description: Canada wants to be the EU's first "associate member," but the EU has no such status. It's a generational pivot toward Europe and away from the US — and Europe's economy grows at half America's pace.
item.content:encoded:
Canada wants to be the EU's first "associate member," but the EU has no such status. It's a generational pivot toward Europe and away from the US — and Europe's economy grows at half America's pace.

Medium information density, but the nonexistent "associate member" status, Carney's European network and reading group, and the EU's Brexit-driven red line are three judgments you won't hear anywhere else.

0:00 Canada wants to be the EU's first associate member, but the status doesn't exist
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Canada is negotiating to become an associate member of the EU. But the show says it plainly: the EU has no such thing as an "associate member" — you're either a member, paying into the budget, accepting free movement of people and seamless truck crossings, or you're not. All 27 current members are in Europe, sharing borders, regulations, and mostly the euro. So what Canada gets will be a status invented for it, with details still under negotiation. What Carney wants isn't another buyer but a group of "like-minded" countries to build, together, the institutions and technological capabilities that America's "wrecking ball" can't reach.

3:01 Canada once saw itself as Europeans living in North America
This isn't a new idea; it's a return to an old identity. In the first half of the 20th century, some Canadians genuinely saw themselves as "Europeans living in North America" — today's oldest Canadians were born British subjects, and Canada didn't open an embassy in Washington until the 1920s. On the eve of World War II, Canada's trade with Britain still exceeded its trade with the US. After the war America became the center of gravity of the West, the auto industry integrated in the 1960s, NAFTA took effect in 1994, and Canadian elites switched from going to Oxford and Cambridge to going to Harvard and Yale. Trump's tensions reopened a forgotten historical question: where do Canadians belong in the world?

6:13 The 51st state isn't a trade negotiation, it's a sovereignty question
When Trump returned for a second term, he didn't just want to renegotiate a trade deal; he questioned the territorial integrity of allies like Canada and Denmark, and said openly he wanted Canada to become the 51st state. The show's judgment: if it were only a trade renegotiation, you could negotiate; once sovereignty is touched, you're touching something highly emotional, sensitive, electorally meaningful and bound up with a country's self-image. One Canadian official, after reading every Trump biography he could find, concluded that the 51st-state talk was "price discovery" — throwing out an outrageous idea to test the reaction. Whatever the intent, the effect was real: Carney went from trailing by 25 points in the polls to winning, overnight.

8:17 Carney defined the trade war as "we are being attacked"
Carney had two signature moments after taking office. One was the Davos speech, landing right in the middle of the Greenland crisis, with Trump due to speak the next day; Carney went first and delivered the clearest anti-Trumpist manifesto yet: Canadians' old comfortable assumption that geography and alliances automatically deliver prosperity and security no longer holds. The second came when the US imposed tariffs — instead of backing down, he escalated, hitting back with tariffs of his own, and he still wouldn't budge after the final round of trade talks collapsed. Asked at a press conference why it felt like war was about to start today, his answer was: "Because we are being attacked." The show says that for a technocrat and centrist to escalate is counterintuitive, and that is precisely what makes him seen as the leader of the Western-allies-against-Trump movement — for better or worse.

11:22 Carney's European network matters more than his policies
A prime minister of a North American country has an unusually large number of European friends: a doctorate in economics from Oxford, the first foreigner to run the Bank of England. Macron was a banker, German Chancellor Merz worked at BlackRock, Finnish President Stubb also came from finance — Carney knows them all. In Ottawa he also has a reading group whose members are political heavyweights and industry leaders, and someone has a Fight Club-style rule: "The first rule of reading group is you don't talk about reading group." Most of them were educated at Oxford or Cambridge, are familiar with Europe, and remain in touch with the prime minister, feeding him exactly the kind of ideas about how to bring Canada closer to Europe. The show says interviewees were far more secretive about the reading group than about Canada's plan to join the EU.

14:27 The talks aren't just trade — they're data cables and Erasmus
What the two sides are discussing goes far beyond tariffs: laying data cables connecting Europe and Canada; jointly building data centers, cloud storage and satellite networks placed beyond the reach of American tech giants; building new pipelines in Canada to send natural gas to the East Coast and on to Europe; using icebreakers to open an Arctic route for fertilizer. They also plan to entwine Canadian and EU research institutions to create an academic and scientific output network that can rival the American system. Canada is even pushing to join the EU's Erasmus student-exchange program — the show says that's a big deal in Europe, and that it has produced many marriages. If a generation of Canadians goes to school in Paris, Spain and Italy, and a generation of Italians comes to Ottawa, Montreal and Vancouver, then what's being discussed isn't just economics but social ties deeper than the flow of natural gas and minerals.

17:45 The EU's red line: no one can think you can quit and still get the benefits
For Europe, Canada is a "shiny new toy": it has raw materials, critical minerals and energy Europe has long coveted, its values are similar, and Carney speaking French and English and making his first trip to Paris and London rather than Washington means a lot to Europeans. But the risks are just as clear. The EU is haunted by Brexit, and its long-standing red line is that "no one can ever be allowed to think they can leave the club and keep enjoying the benefits" — if big countries start quitting and demanding a Canada-style deal, that would be fatal to the EU. So the puzzle Carney has to solve is: get Canada a large share of the trade and connectivity benefits without creating a precedent that lets a country like Italy say, "We don't like these regulations — let's leave and be a Canada-style member, no rules but all the benefits."

19:54 The real pain hasn't arrived yet; the White House bets geography is destiny
There are concerns inside Canada: how much sovereignty would joining an ambiguous associate membership cost, which regulations would it accept, what happens to immigration — conservative voters and mainstream newspaper columnists are all asking. But the bigger fear is the cost of decoupling from the US, because so far it's only a war of words and the real pain hasn't hit the Canadian economy: two-thirds of exports depend on the US, and that's a lot of people's businesses and jobs. The White House's judgment is that geography is destiny, Canada is right there, decades of economic ties are real, and in the end they will pull Canada back to the table — the flirtation with Europe can't change economic reality. You can't force Canadian businesses to do business in Europe, when a few miles across the border (kilometers, in Canada) sits an attractive market.

item.title: Ranking Psychology's Classic Experiments: Many Findings Don't Survive Replication
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-verybad-心理学经典实验排等级-很多结论撑不过复现/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-verybad-心理学经典实验排等级-很多结论撑不过复现/
item.description: The Milgram shock experiment still replicates, which is absurd enough on its own; and the Good Samaritan experiment had only 40 subjects total, so even if they got it right, they got it right by accident.
item.content:encoded:
The Milgram shock experiment still replicates, which is absurd enough on its own; and the Good Samaritan experiment had only 40 subjects total, so even if they got it right, they got it right by accident.

Two philosophers and a psychologist rank classic studies from D to S, and along the way settle accounts with the replication crisis, Zimbardo's fraudulent original notes, and small samples.

10:08 Milgram still replicating is itself absurd
Milgram recruited New Haven workers in a Yale basement, led them to believe they were shocking another person, with the voltage labeled up to 300 volts and marked dangerous; the person being "shocked" was actually a trained actor, and about 65% of them pressed all the way to the end. He ran a large number of variants, manipulating whether the experimenter wore a white coat, the distance to the person being shocked, and which university's name was on the door. The study directly rewrote psychology's ethics review system; today this kind of experiment can't be done. Dave says that a social psychology study from the 50s or 60s that still replicates is itself "[ __ ] banana," which is why it goes in the S tier — he's using replication as the bar, not fame.

29:20 The Good Samaritan experiment had only 40 people
Darley and Batson had seminary students go to the other side of campus to deliver the parable of the Good Samaritan, with a person who was visibly injured and groaning for help placed along the way; the manipulated variable was the time pressure they were under. It turned out that time pressure predicted whether they stopped to help better than what topic they were going to speak on. But Dave points out that the whole experiment had only 40 subjects total, and after splitting into groups the samples were tiny. He groups this kind of study with the telephone booth coin experiment as a common disease of 60s and 70s social psychology: severely underpowered, "even if they were right, they were right by accident." Paul says it's great as material for making people reflect on human nature, but as a scientific finding he doesn't trust it, and gives it a D.

48:38 On the cloth mother, mothers already knew
Harlow separated infant monkeys from their mothers and built two surrogate mothers: a wire frame with a bottle attached, and a soft, huggable cloth mother that provided no milk. Except when they had to nurse, the infants stayed on the cloth mother the rest of the time. This refuted the behaviorist explanation that infants love their mothers because the mother provides food, and supported the role of contact comfort. The episode clarifies that Harlow did not shock the monkeys; what's hard to watch is the image of frightened infants lunging at the cloth mother and clinging on for dear life. He also called the isolation device the "pit of despair" and the restraint device the "rape rack" in published articles, and the reaction on the show was "he's just a psychopath." Tamler argues for the lowest score, not because of cruelty, but because these studies didn't show anything any mother would know by intuition the moment you asked her.

1:10:52 The prison experiment's author was coaching guards to abuse
The original notes and recordings dug up on the Stanford prison experiment show that Zimbardo himself was coaching the people randomly assigned to be guards to engage in abusive behavior. If the intended story of the study is "put people in this role and they spontaneously become sadists," then on the available evidence that conclusion is highly suspect — he didn't report how much he pushed them. David considers this close to scientific fraud, groups it with "dog torturers," and no longer teaches it. But David also cautions: across the Milgram and Asch series, people differ, and some said "screw you, I'm not doing it" at the lowest shock level. Tamler adds that when he interviewed Zimbardo, the latter talked about Milgram, saying Milgram did no psychological screening and some of the people who came in might have been sociopaths, while Zimbardo claimed he did screen — using that to prove these were normal people.

1:15:59 Even adults fail the false belief task
The false belief task comes from Premack and Woodruff's paper "Does the Chimpanzee Have a Theory of Mind"; Dennett proposed this design in a commentary: Sally puts a toy in a box and leaves, Anne moves it to a basket, and you ask where Sally will look when she comes back. Children before age three or four say the place where the toy actually is, and around age five they start getting it right; this shift from failure to success is one of the most robust findings in all of developmental psychology. But Paul and Susan Birch tested adults and found that adults find it hard too — there's an immediate intuition pointing at "where the thing actually is" that has to be inhibited; he demonstrates it live in his intro course, and about a third of the students get it wrong. What bothers Tamler is that once the paradigm got hot, the whole field shifted from that interesting question to the methodology itself, and the test became the construct.

1:24:06 To deny the methods are all broken, you have to accept ESP
