Mark Gurman is the most accurate reporter on Apple, and this episode strings executive turnover, the AI roadmap, the privacy controversy and foldable predictions into one line, with high information density.

5:09 The biggest difference between Ternus and Cook is willingness to decide
Gurman says the event was almost interchangeable with the Cook era, with the one difference that Ternus opened by laying out a view on AI. The mechanism he gives is management style: you bring an idea to Cook and he keeps probing with questions, in many cases not making a single decision, it's a collective decision; you bring it to Ternus and he gives you a decision, gives you an opinion, you may hate the opinion, but he takes a position. Gurman stresses this is exactly the biggest difference between the two men from talking to insiders, and it explains why Ternus talked about AI first thing on stage.

8:20 The 2026 event had not one new AI feature
Gurman points out that Apple held a big product event in September 2026 and launched no notable new AI features, with the opening 15 minutes or so just retelling the past two years of Apple Intelligence. His explanation: Apple has gone as far on AI as it can and can only tell the best story with the cards it holds; and Apple has no AI-centric device, so it has to prop up the iPhone as its AI device until a killer device appears and it can change the narrative.

13:29 Under Cook, Apple became an institution
Gurman distinguishes the Cook era from the Jobs era: in the Cook era people's relationship with Apple is a relationship with an institution, one that spans the globe and is enormous, like IBM; the Jobs era was one new product after another redefining categories. He also corrects the host's read on Vision Pro — every time he writes that Vision Pro is on life support, he gets dozens of reactions close to death-threat level, because some people have built businesses around spatial computing and some consumers paid four thousand dollars for it.

20:45 Apple spent five years swapping out the old guard one by one
Gurman reconstructs the rhythm of the handover: in 2023 Cook began saying at every executive meeting that succession had to be taken seriously; at the time the top ranks either had five hundred million in the bank or were billionaires, and were close in age. So they lined up an order and went one by one — at the end of 2024 CFO Luca Maestri retired, replaced by Kevin Parekh; in 2025 COO Jeff Williams retired, succeeded by his deputy; in 2026 the general counsel changed, with Jennifer Newstead poached from Meta; and only at the end of 2026 did Cook hand off to Ternus. Gurman calls this retention strategy Hotel California: you can never leave.

28:07 The chip chief was kept with a title invented on the spot
Gurman says the second most important person at Apple now is the hardware head, who built Apple Silicon, Apple's key differentiator. In late summer or early autumn last year he went to tell Cook he was quitting, right in the middle of preparations for Ternus to take over. Cook got him to stay and take part in the transition, promising him the title of chief hardware officer, which Apple had never had, letting him keep his existing team and also take over Ternus's side of the business. Gurman judges this is not a long-term arrangement, and that the man already wants to leave again — he conquered the Mac, shed Intel and Qualcomm, and Apple has no next goal, so he may leave within a year or two, at which point the hardware engineering team will have to be split up again, because no successor carries his industry weight.

33:15 Willing to spend tens of billions on a modem, but says it needn't own AI
What Gurman finds most absurd is executives saying in interviews over the past year that ‘we never owned search, we don't need to own AI’. He counters: these are two completely different things, and Apple spent tens of billions to own a cellular modem that had already been commoditised, buying and fixing Intel's modem business — willing to do that for a modem but unwilling to own AI is ridiculous. The internal idea was originally to work with Google as a stopgap until it could build its own models, but Gurman says he has seen no evidence that Apple is restarting its own model effort, making big AI acquisitions, or paying AI researchers top salaries.

48:53 The watch's always-on transcription stepped on the privacy landmine
Gurman's reaction to the Apple Watch's always-on listening feature was ‘I can't believe they did it’. The feature only transcribes, doesn't record or store, and a double tap shows you the last 15 seconds of what someone said to you, without their consent. He says Apple knows the next-generation interface needs some degree of ambient capture, but the societal privacy problem is unsolved: technical white papers, private cloud compute and encryption can't hold back the social backlash. He thinks Apple could have put audio and visual intelligence together next year and told one coherent privacy story; as it is, it's boiling the frog slowly.

57:05 Foldables will become the new normal within a decade
Gurman offers a bold prediction: foldables will become the new normal within a decade. He draws an analogy with smartphone penetration — at the end of 2006 smartphones were about 6% of the market, now they're 85%, and they crossed half in five or six years; the iPhone itself wasn't the source of that, but it pulled everyone into the smartphone game, and he thinks the iPhone Duo will do the same for the phone market. He also mentions the iPhone's number-transfer feature, hinting the future may be a combination of a foldable for work and a smaller, lighter phone for weekends with family.

item.title: The Real Bottleneck in the Treasury Market: Not Size, but Not Enough Intermediaries
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-macromusings-美债市场真正的瓶颈-不是规模-是中间商不够用了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-macromusings-美债市场真正的瓶颈-不是规模-是中间商不够用了/
item.description: Primary dealers' balance sheets long ago stopped keeping pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries, and market makers have ceded ground to high-frequency traders — who then collectively retreated in March 2020. That is the core of the Treasury liquidity problem.
item.content:encoded:
Primary dealers' balance sheets long ago stopped keeping pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries, and market makers have ceded ground to high-frequency traders — who then collectively retreated in March 2020. That is the core of the Treasury liquidity problem.

A front-line operator at the New York Fed explains Treasury market structure, with empirical data from two 2025 papers and the latest TBAC developments. High information density.

11:26 The Treasury market is so big it has to attract new buyers
Golay gives the scale: CBO counts $30 trillion in outstanding Treasuries at the end of 2025, and projects another $26 trillion to $27 trillion over the next decade. The market splits into two parts — the cash market (buying and selling Treasuries directly, partly through electronic inter-dealer broker trading and partly dealer-to-client) and the repo market (borrowing against Treasuries as collateral, intermediated mainly by dealers). A market this large and growing necessarily has to attract different types of investors, including high-frequency traders and hedge funds that are more sensitive to price.

14:31 High-frequency traders went from zero to the main force in electronic markets
Golay calls these firms principal trading firms (PTFs); they mostly run high-frequency strategies and trade on electronic platforms. Twenty years ago they were not in the Treasury market at all; today they may account for the majority of electronic cash market trading. The turning point was the 2014 flash rally — yields swung sharply and no one could explain why, which is when the official sector began to truly understand how PTFs had grown in electronic markets, and it also sparked the IAWG's work on market structure and getting better data.

16:33 Primary dealer balance sheets have not kept up with the growth in outstanding Treasuries
Golay cites a chart from a Darrell Duffie paper: the size of primary dealers' balance sheets devoted to intermediating Treasuries has simply not kept pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries. Part of that is post-2008 reforms, and part is just how fast the stock itself has grown. The result is that the market has had to attract more price-sensitive types of investors. She also corrects a common impression: it is not that PTFs always retreat during volatility — in other volatile periods the official sector has observed PTFs increasing their activity; but in March 2020, everyone pulled back.

19:42 The essence of all-to-all is bypassing dealer matching
All-to-all trading is literally that: any participant in the Treasury market can trade with any other participant. That is nothing new in the equity market, but much of the Treasury market is over-the-counter and dealer-intermediated, so it is not the case there. Golay points out that entering the March 2020 crisis, dealers already had a lot of Treasuries piled up on their balance sheets, so when the wave of selling hit there was no intermediation capacity left. If you could find a counterparty to match with without going through a dealer, that might ease things. But she says plainly that at the time most people were selling, and it is hard to imagine all-to-all perfectly solving that situation — it is just that every incremental improvement helps.

22:51 All-to-all is stuck on the lack of counterparty matching
One of the paper's core findings: in the off-the-run market, if you look at a 15-minute window, almost no one wants to buy the same off-the-run security you want to sell. Stretch the window to a day and the match rate rises to 60% to 70%. Golay mentions possible directions for innovation, such as an end-of-day batch auction; some institutions already have this capability. But to date, no case in this area has really gotten off the ground successfully. She also notes that expanding central clearing could push the transition to all-to-all, because you would not need a bilateral clearing arrangement with every counterparty — you would only need to connect to a central counterparty.

29:06 Off-the-run is 97% of the stock but a liquidity backwater
Off-the-run refers to older Treasuries, ranging from those issued three months ago to 29- and 30-year issues, and they make up about 97% of outstanding Treasuries. The selling in the March 2020 dash for cash was mainly off-the-run, and the off-the-run market is dealer-intermediated, with no all-to-all. Golay and colleagues at the Board of Governors and the New York Fed did empirical work using TRACE data collected by FINRA, and the transaction-level data is visible only to the official sector. The conclusion: the older the Treasury, the worse its liquidity — larger price impact, lower volume, wider bid-ask spreads.

31:15 The cheapest to deliver can revive liquidity
Another finding of the paper: when an off-the-run Treasury becomes the cheapest to deliver into a Treasury futures contract, its liquidity is better than that of comparable off-the-run issues. This suggests the off-the-run problem is partly about trading activity itself — where there is trading activity, liquidity improves; where there is none, liquidity deteriorates. On policy implications, Golay mentions that Treasury buybacks can create trading activity around off-the-run issues and improve liquidity; central clearing makes clearing smoother; and as for reducing the number of issuance dates and making individual issues larger, the paper reaches no conclusion, because investors also like the finer granularity of monthly issuance.

36:33 TBAC put the brakes on expanding transparency
At a recent TBAC meeting, a member suggested expanding transparency around Treasury trading data: there is already market-wide aggregate statistics, plus transaction-level data for on-the-run issues; the suggestion was to consider publishing transaction-level data for Treasury bills, and more frequent on-the-run data. But TBAC expressed caution about expanding transparency in other areas, including the off-the-run and TIPS markets. Golay says this is interesting, because data transparency has been a focus of the IAWG's work in recent years and was listed as a priority in 2021. She personally thinks small incremental transparency is beneficial, but understands that in less liquid markets, releasing too much information can make intermediation very difficult.

item.title: Stanford Has a Secret Course That Teaches 12 People How to Extract Value From Other Humans
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-grayarea-斯坦福有一门秘密课程-教12个人如何从他人身上提取价值/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-grayarea-斯坦福有一门秘密课程-教12个人如何从他人身上提取价值/
item.category: The Gray Area with Sean Illing
item.description: The course isn't in the catalog, admits only 12 students a year, and is taught by a Silicon Valley CEO on how to extract value from people. The author says students lying isn't an accident — it's what the machine has long rewarded.
item.content:encoded:
The course isn't in the catalog, admits only 12 students a year, and is taught by a Silicon Valley CEO on how to extract value from people. The author says students lying isn't an accident — it's what the machine has long rewarded.

Not a vague critique of Silicon Valley but a specific investigation with course names, dollar figures and people's names; if you care about early-stage investing and talent pipelines, the detail density is high.

5:12 You can raise hundreds of thousands before you have a company
Pre-idea funding was the newest layer of the game when Theo arrived on campus: give an 18-year-old who just started school hundreds of thousands, even millions, of dollars, sign a one-page SAFE check, agree that "if you start a company later, come back to us" — otherwise the money never has to be repaid. For a VC it's pocket change; they don't really believe in these hyped-up teenagers, and they don't need you personally to succeed — they just need one overnight sensation. Meanwhile students are encouraged to make enormous promises and then discover again and again that no one follows up: lie, and there are no consequences.

13:22 The secret course teaches extracting value
Stanford has a course that isn't in the catalog, called How to Rule the World, taught by a Silicon Valley CEO who styles himself a professor, admitting only 12 students a year — merely knowing it exists is a status symbol. Its central assignment is extracting value from people, with a strong flavor of the ends justifying the means. One woman Theo interviewed said the course taught her how to lie to VCs to raise money — she later actually raised millions and dropped out of Stanford, despite having already been caught cheating in a computer science class; a few months later she put out a glossy launch video for a technology that didn't exist, and Silicon Valley cheered her on anyway, she moved into a mansion, and she was invited back to Stanford to speak.

26:46 Ethics isn't a premise; getting caught is what counts
During ethics week in the intro computer science course, the professor discussed a case where a software defect killed four people on a radiation therapy machine, and the TA asked who in the room cared about ethics — Theo was the only one who raised his hand. Weeks later a classmate told him he was taking a business ethics course, and "we're all just there to figure out how they got caught." He didn't sense these people needed to pretend to care; when Sam Bankman-Fried was under house arrest in the house on the Stanford campus where he grew up, students made pilgrimages, threw parties themed around him, and said they wanted to replicate his success minus the final fall. A colleague's summary of the money that mysteriously vanished at Tree Hacks: it's all just a little bit of fraud.

38:01 The real reason the president fell wasn't the data
Board members who ousted Marc Tessier-Lavigne later told Theo that one of the heaviest reasons they gave was his posture — a highly aggressive public stance when challenged, deny, deny, deny, plus the threatening letters sent by the lawyer he hired, Steve Neal, which embarrassed the university. Theo found no evidence he personally falsified data: the problem was in the labs he oversaw, where subordinates fabricated data in papers he co-authored, including the 2009 paper claiming to have found the cause of Alzheimer's, while internal company results before publication showed its central finding was "at best unreliable." He was asked to retract and refused, dragging it out for a decade. What drove him out was image management, not the data.

39:01 The mansion closed four days after he was ousted
Four days after the board unanimously removed him, Tessier-Lavigne closed on a 7,600-square-foot mansion in "America's most expensive zip code," valued at over $10 million; eight months later he announced he had raised $1 billion for a new company doing AI biotech. Of the two VCs that led the round, an investor at one messaged Theo two months later to rib him, followed by a winking emoji; an investor at the other offered him money to start a company. Theo says it's the most Silicon Valley thing you can imagine: everything can be monetized, even taking down a university president turns into an invitation.

45:44 Duck syndrome: paddling like mad under the surface
Duck syndrome is a term Stanford coined itself: students glide across the surface elegantly, seeming to do everything effortlessly, while underneath their two legs paddle like mad just to keep from sinking. Katie Meyer was its best illustration — women's soccer captain, led the team to an NCAA title, headed to law school, didn't drink, didn't smoke, didn't speed. A few months before graduation, late on a Friday night, after every student support office had closed, she received a letter: because six months earlier she had spilled coffee on a football player (she said it was an accident, he said it was intentional), her degree was suspended. That night she took her own life. Twelve schools later paid tribute to her; Stanford was not among them. The women's soccer team she had just captained held a mental health night and didn't mention her name.

52:01 A legendary professor's fraud case, and the school says it never heard of it
Stan Cohen was the first geneticist to transplant a gene from one living organism into another, and his 1970s and '80s recombinant DNA technology gave rise to the model of universities making money from patents; in its last valid year, that patent contributed 62% of all of Stanford's patent revenue. In his freshman year, Theo looked him up and found he had been found liable for fraud by a court: he had promised investors a drug target that might cure Huntington's disease, and said the drug was already approved to treat another disease, without telling them it had been permanently banned by the FDA in 1976 because it was lethal. He was ultimately ordered to pay $29 million and paid it. Theo asked the university, and the university replied that it had never heard of the case and had no involvement whatsoever — even though Stanford owned the relevant intellectual property and had been subpoenaed by the court.

55:04 Raising money is easier than an internship, and that itself is a signal
The saying circulating in Stanford's inner circles is that raising money for a startup is easier than getting an internship — Theo says that's absurd, it shouldn't be that way, but that's the status quo. He describes the moment as a game of AI musical chairs: everyone is waiting to see who's still standing when the music stops and who's left holding the bag. He isn't worried about cash-flow-positive companies like Meta and Google; he's worried about the companies clinging to the AI narrative that have no technology of their own, no revenue, and no ability to generate revenue — they can't hold on, and they will collapse. But he also cautions that Silicon Valley hasn't held power for long, that it's a very immature power system that hasn't grown guardrails, transparency or accountability, and that one collapse doesn't necessarily mean a reckoning.

item.title: America's Manufacturing Hollowing Isn't a Capability Problem, It's a Financial Return Problem
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-oddlots-美国制造业空心化不是能力问题-是金融回报问题/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-oddlots-美国制造业空心化不是能力问题-是金融回报问题/
item.description: Chris Power says America manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statements, while China manages it like national security; tariffs are just an imperfect corrective tool, and the core issue is getting American consumers to stop subsidizing competitors' industrial capacity.
item.content:encoded:
Chris Power says America manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statements, while China manages it like national security; tariffs are just an imperfect corrective tool, and the core issue is getting American consumers to stop subsidizing competitors' industrial capacity.

Two frontline hardware founders explain the real bottlenecks of American reindustrialization: not technology, but trust, cost, and supply chain definitions. High information density; the second half on tariffs and subsidies is the most valuable.

2:02 The reserve currency is the first step of decline
Chris Power gives a four-step cycle: great powers first have a generative population and the best industrial capacity, then win or prevent a war, then become extremely lazy, and finally outsource the very things that made them successful. He says this cycle repeats roughly every 150 years: the Dutch gave way to the British, the British to the Americans, and each time industrial power was re-traded for financial power, the world's reserve currency changed. This judgment was the starting point for him founding Hadrian: you think you're Mike Tyson at his peak, but your opponent thinks you're the Mike Tyson before Buster Douglas knocked him out.

9:10 90% of the factory floor is a software problem
Chris Power says the biggest misconception about advanced manufacturing is that seeing people moving things in a factory means it's a humanoid robot problem. In reality, 90% of advanced manufacturing is smart people sitting at computers doing digital engineering, or operating an extremely dumb computer on the shop floor. Welders or machinists have to stand in front of the machine because the system isn't closed-loop; they do trigonometry in their heads to judge whether the tool is about to break. So Hadrian positions itself as a software company, breaking physical tasks into high-judgment setups and then handing them to robots, CNC, or welding systems.

14:14 Software is done in Silicon Valley, hardware in LA
Tom Mueller says the aerospace talent ecosystem in Southern California is recovering; three or four years after SpaceX was founded in 2002, the aerospace employment curve in the South Bay started to rise. He lists what's happening simultaneously in the region: nuclear energy companies, drone companies, defense companies, 3D printing companies, and Anduril in Orange County. The two companies poach from each other and compete for talent; Northrop Grumman is right across the street from Impulse. Tom's summary: software is done in Silicon Valley, hardware in LA.

15:17 Vertical integration is to learn the problem, not to save money
Tom Mueller explains the real logic of SpaceX-style vertical integration: you have to build the first development engine or spacecraft yourself, because you need to learn all the assembly and machining problems during prototyping. If you hand it to a machine shop from the start, and the drawings have problems or the parts don't fit, you learn nothing. Once the design converges, you outsource. Chris Power adds that every company should keep 10% to 15% of in-house capacity, because there's always a "hot pot" moment when you need a genius to make something in an hour to meet a flight milestone, but scale must happen externally.

16:18 Outsourcing decisions are about trust, not finance
Chris Power says what's bought and sold in manufacturing is trust. Hadrian's vertical integration strategy is to outsource as much as possible to every reindustrialization startup and small business, because there are too many projects to run. But they vertically integrate the links where they "don't believe you can deliver on time." This isn't a financial trade-off; they'd rather spend an extra two million dollars on equipment and hire a team than bet on a traditional foundry that has been late on every submarine project for the past thirty years. His exact words: most of America is incompetent at trust and scheduling.

19:20 In WWII, America was China
Chris Power uses WWII as an analogy: German engineers crushed America on engineering, but America wore them down with McDonald's-style mass production and better logistics. He says America played the role in WWII that China plays today—not by having the best engineering, but by producing the most. Now the situation is reversed: US missile stockpiles run out in seven days in war games, China built 2,600 ships while America built six. His conclusion: you can have the best Raytheon missiles, but if you can't mass-produce them, you have no options.

21:23 The robot bottleneck is training data velocity
Chris Power says the robot competition ultimately depends on software, and software, especially AI, now depends on training data velocity, which in turn depends on physical world deployment—i.e., mass manufacturing. So this isn't a friendly competition between American companies over "whether Tesla sells more Optimus or Google wins"; it's a civilization-level confrontation. Tom Mueller adds from the space angle: building on the Moon and Mars requires robot legions, not humans, because the environment is too dangerous and too expensive; a good robot needs three things—dexterous hands, vision which is basically solved, and an AI brain.

29:40 Tariffs are an imperfect corrective tool
Chris Power says manufacturing has four inputs: energy, labor, cost of capital, and export tariffs. He has done the math: even if Hadrian's labor and energy costs were zero, importing components from China would still be three times cheaper than buying raw materials in America and making them yourself. He believes China has run industrial policy as national security since 1985, subsidizing energy, labor, capital, and export tariffs, while America manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statement returns. The problem with tariffs is enforcement: banning only China but not Singapore means Chinese companies route through Singapore; differences in definitions of raw materials and assembly also hurt American companies importing components from Mexico.

item.title: He Cooked the Chickpea Pasta Into Mush, Then Survived by Telling People to Steep It Like Tea
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-howibuilt-把鹰嘴豆意面煮成糊后-他靠-像泡茶一样泡-活了下来/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-howibuilt-把鹰嘴豆意面煮成糊后-他靠-像泡茶一样泡-活了下来/
item.description: Banza's first scaled-up production run failed across the board — 20,000 boxes of pasta fell apart the moment they hit boiling water. They didn't destroy them. They slapped on a sticker that said "steep it like tea" and shipped — because not shipping meant losing the retailer forever.
item.content:encoded:
Banza's first scaled-up production run failed across the board — 20,000 boxes of pasta fell apart the moment they hit boiling water. They didn't destroy them. They slapped on a sticker that said "steep it like tea" and shipped — because not shipping meant losing the retailer forever.

The founder's account is unusually dense with failure detail: three scrapped production batches, a kidney stone, being thrown out of the factory, a 30% week-over-week decline. Worth hearing for anyone who wants to know how you survive a near-death moment.

5:14 The starting point wasn't a business insight, it was a runny nose
In college Brian's fridge held nothing but hummus, food was just "fuel" to him, and he cycled between antibiotics and steroids for so long he was nearly facing surgery. It was his father, an orthodontist, who got him to try an elimination diet, and that's how he found that wheat-based foods triggered sinus inflammation — one beer and the next day he couldn't breathe. The ENT told him: I don't know what you're talking about, but if it works, keep doing it. That private problem became the product definition: high-protein, high-fiber, gluten-free pasta, doing what Chobani did for yogurt.

10:26 The first recipe had chia in it and was too sticky to look at
He bought Bob's Red Mill chickpea flour on Amazon and followed blogs for combinations. Version one was chickpeas plus eggs plus chia — the chia made it so sticky the result was ugly. With no rolling pin he used a wine bottle; with no pasta cutter he used a knife, dusting flour on the table as he cut to keep it from sticking. Version two dropped the chia, leaving just chickpeas and eggs, and was clearly better, but to make it usable for more people he added back tapioca starch and xanthan gum and committed to a vegan route. His first capital expenditure was an Atlas Mercado hand-crank pasta machine, about $30 on Amazon. He got up at 5 a.m. every day to make pasta, put on country music, and his roommates thought he was insane.

20:49 Going from 200 pounds an hour to 1,000 magnified every mistake
They first found a tiny gluten-free factory in Michigan that could only do 150 to 200 pounds an hour — wildly inefficient, but they could learn as they went. To get into 190 Meijer stores and 2 Eataly locations, that capacity wasn't enough, so they found what was then the largest gluten-free pasta plant in the country, outside Los Angeles. The problem: that plant had only ever run rice and corn pasta, never legumes. Scaled up to roughly 1,000 pounds an hour, the pasta looked fine coming out and turned into total mush the moment it was boiled. Each trial run was 8,000 to 10,000 pounds, and a failure meant the die costs and ingredient costs were gone, while they had only a little over $100,000 on hand.

26:02 He got thrown out of the factory for asking the line operator
After several failed trial runs, Brian ignored the other side's objections and went straight to the operator on the production line to ask what was actually going wrong. The worker said, "This corn smells weird," and he answered: that isn't corn, we're not making corn pasta today, it's chickpeas. He realized on the spot that communication had completely broken down, and right after that he was escorted out of the plant. At the same time the distributor was threatening him: if you don't fulfill this purchase order, you will never work with this retailer again. He later estimated the shipment would cost nearly everything they had.

28:07 The solution was don't boil it — steep it like tea
With nowhere left to turn they started testing: boil one minute, two minutes, three minutes, then stop boiling altogether — bring water to a boil, turn off the heat, and let the pasta sit in the hot water. What came out of steeping was better than what came out of boiling, or at least it didn't fall apart. Brian says he wasn't proud of the product, and it bothered him to sell it under his own brand, but he knew it was life or death. The packaging was already printed, so they could only add a sticker reading "Banza is easier to cook than regular pasta — steep it like tea," and then had people hand-apply it to 20,000 boxes. Once that shipment went out, they immediately pulled out of the big plant and went back to the small one in Michigan.

35:18 The box is orange because every pasta box was blue
They noticed that nearly every pasta package on the shelf at the time was blue — Brian put it as "you'd think they'd colluded." Orange contrasts most strongly with blue, and orange was also the color he'd loved since watching Nickelodeon as a kid, so it became the brand color. The packaging copy involved trade-offs too: putting "chickpeas" in the most prominent spot would scare off a lot of people, and so would gluten-free, so the gluten-free certification went on the side while the front led with high protein and high fiber — making consumers feel this was a product "for me," not a product that was "not for me."

41:31 The glyphosate report cut weekly sales by a third
Moms Across America published a report saying glyphosate residue had been detected in Banza products. Brian saw the Google alert during a one-on-one meeting; he says his heart sank and his mind jumped twenty steps ahead. He wanted to verify first, so he put out only a statement saying "we are investigating" — which was nowhere near enough for the most panicked people. Lab results were delayed again and again, dragging on for three weeks. The final published result was 98% below the allegation, but not zero — still a very low level, and below the EWG's risk benchmark. He decided to make the supply chain 100% traceable and to join the Detox Project's certification program.

52:15 Natural channel recovered far more slowly than conventional
The sales recovery was a mixed bag: some channels came back better than before, but the natural channel recovered much more slowly — and that was exactly the customer base with the best repeat purchase rates and the highest sales per store. Brian says it actually makes sense, because natural channel consumers are the most susceptible to this kind of information. What he does now: he keeps alerts on for anywhere Banza and glyphosate are mentioned, and personally goes onto Reddit to reply and add context, with the goal of making it impossible for the story to be seen without its context. He also admits he should have acknowledged what was happening faster and more visibly at the time.

item.title: AI Won't Replace People — What Replaces Them Is Work Nobody Wrote Down
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-twentyvc-ai-不会取代人-取代人的是没被写下来的工作/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-twentyvc-ai-不会取代人-取代人的是没被写下来的工作/
item.description: Models are interchangeable; what's actually valuable is the manual a company writes of its own workflows — that "map of work" is the irreplaceable asset of the AI era, and the only precondition for a company to train its own models.
item.content:encoded:
Models are interchangeable; what's actually valuable is the manual a company writes of its own workflows — that "map of work" is the irreplaceable asset of the AI era, and the only precondition for a company to train its own models.

Daniel Dines breaks down the real bottleneck of AI inside the enterprise from UiPath's front-line view, with a high density of counter-consensus claims — suited to anyone trying to judge the pace of enterprise AI adoption.

6:17 AI does not change its own weights on the job
Daniel argues the biggest difference between AI and humans is not reasoning ability, but that AI does not change its own weights on the job. A human is changed by a job; AI just writes things into a notepad. He gives the example of two chefs: one who has cooked Japanese cuisine for 20 years, one who has cooked Italian for 20 years — give them the same recipe and what they produce is completely different. This is not something you can replicate by writing the company down on paper, because human judgment comes from years of being reshaped by the work. So on the claim that "there are millions of Einsteins in the data center," Daniel thinks what Dario meant is that there are millions of entities with partial reasoning ability — not Einsteins who can learn on the job the way a person does.

16:29 Probabilistic tech shouldn't do work that demands precision
Daniel raises another limit on AI: precision. Every step AI takes is probabilistic — even if each step is 99% correct, after 100 steps the overall success rate may be only 60%. So if you have AI do long multiplication over and over, it will eventually get it wrong. His conclusion: just because a tool can do something doesn't mean you should use it for that thing. ChatGPT looks like it is doing arithmetic, but behind the scenes it is calling a computer tool — the precision is not coming from ChatGPT. Extend that logic to the enterprise: all work that demands precision should run on precise technology; there is no reason for it to run on probabilistic technology.

18:34 Deploying AI hasn't gotten easier; deploying automation has
Daniel points to an asymmetry inside the enterprise: deploying AI agents is not easier than it was two years ago, but deploying automation has become much easier, because you can use coding agents to generate the automation. He lists ChatGPT, chain of thoughts and coding agents as the three main milestones. Coding agents work at "design time": people use them to build automation that runs precisely every time at "execution time"; and when automation breaks because an upstream system changed, AI can come back and fix it. The result is that AI is generating the software that runs the company, and that software cannot change its behavior in real time — it can be audited, tested and read by people. This is the pattern he sees taking shape in the enterprise right now.

23:46 Blind layoffs cut the people AI most needs
In his book Daniel puts forward the concept of the "credentialed middle": companies used to hire for deep domain credentials in some field, and that is exactly the kind of expertise AI helps with most. His judgment is counterintuitive — you will be inclined to cut the people who are not the biggest experts in the domain, but those are precisely the people you will need to supplement expert work with AI. He gives the example of a law firm: it used to hire 25 interns a year, this year it hired only 4. He agrees most roles will need fewer people, but the key question is "which people." His criterion: keep the ones with the most initiative, who can maintain client relationships, who can mentor newcomers, who carry the company culture — because AI cannot show initiative in the human sense.

25:51 What decides whether AI can take over is how clear the framework is
Harry argues that work like finance and accounting is highly verifiable, so it is easy for AI to replace. Daniel disagrees outright: it is not a question of verifiability, but of whether the job is framed by a framework someone else has already defined. He says finance is precisely a domain where the framework is unclear — receive an invoice or an order and there can be different ways to handle it, such as whether Nvidia would ship to OpenAI first, and that rule may never have been written down at all. If the rules are not captured by a framework, AI cannot learn them. So a company must first hand the "map of work" to AI: all workflows, all exceptions, all processes, all systems. This is also what he keeps stressing: models are interchangeable — the map of work and the processes around it are where the real value lies.

29:01 Use agents to interview employees and draw the work as a map
UiPath has launched a technology called cartography, as a discipline that helps companies surface how work actually gets done. Concretely, it uses a product called a cartographer agent to interview real business experts and have them record what they are doing, with the agent following up in real time: why did you change how you handled this invoice because the zip code was different? Why did you take another path? That is how exceptions get dug out one by one. Then it aggregates data across multiple people to generate a real-time process map. With that "map of work" in hand, you then use coding agents to design how the process should be transformed, and ultimately, through "printing software," push the process from purely manual point A toward a state where fewer people operate the system and more automation and agentic AI operate it.

34:15 Vibe coding is easy for prototypes, hard for production
Daniel admits UiPath tried vibe coding: at first it looked astonishing, but pushing it into production hit a wall — connectors, permissions, auditing, security, all of it has to be maintained. He gives his own example of writing a procurement tool: initially written entirely by AI, but the database schema was completely wrong and someone had to rebuild the structure. His conclusion is that going from prototype to production is where the real work is, not writing the code itself. In the end you will likely pay as much as, or more than, the tool you replaced — while also consuming the bandwidth of your best people. So he does not think systems of record like Salesforce will be replaced by vibe coding.

45:34 The legal AI opportunity is in process, not model calls
Harry runs the numbers: the US legal industry is a $300 billion market, and if 30% of the labor can be replaced, that is $90 billion in revenue. Daniel counters that the $90 billion will not convert into token revenue — maybe only 10%, so a $10 billion token opportunity. His judgment: for legal opinions, open-source models and frontier models are both good enough; what is actually valuable is the custom workflow built around the legal process. If Harvey and Lagora just call a model once for you to get a legal opinion, that will not be a hundred-billion-dollar market; but if they really draw the work as a map, build the workflows, and build you a legal department, the value is far greater.

item.title: Legal-Cannabis States Aren't Safe Either: A Federal Ban Is About to Empty the THC Shelves
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-indicator-大麻合法州也躲不过-联邦禁令要清空-thc-货架/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-indicator-大麻合法州也躲不过-联邦禁令要清空-thc-货架/
item.description: A loophole in the 2018 farm bill let hemp-derived THC grow into a $28 billion industry. Now Congress wants to close it — and even legal-cannabis states will feel it when they lose the cheap alternative.
item.content:encoded:
A loophole in the 2018 farm bill let hemp-derived THC grow into a $28 billion industry. Now Congress wants to close it — and even legal-cannabis states will feel it when they lose the cheap alternative.

Eight minutes on how a regulatory loophole became an industry and how it gets cut off in one stroke — for anyone watching policy risk and regulatory arbitrage.

0:00 Legal-cannabis states don't escape a federal ban
Recreational cannabis is legal in half of US states, but the reason THC drinks, vapes and gummies can be sold openly in states that ban cannabis is a loophole left by the 2018 farm bill: it allows low-concentration THC from hemp. After lab processing, that low concentration is enough to mimic a cannabis high, which is how you get Delta 8, Delta 9 — and, as the show jokes, by now Delta 11. Congress now wants to close the loophole, and it's using a stricter ban to do it. The key point is that this is a federal ban, so even if your state has legal cannabis, you get hit.

1:00 What's being banned is a $28 billion industry
The show puts the size at $28 billion and says the industry could disappear before the end of this year. Tennessee has already gone first: since July it has banned most THC hemp products, and a local reporter describes herself as already living in a ‘post-hemp world’. State legislators even beat Congress to it, banning full-spectrum CBD and smokable flower first. For retailers, farmers and processors, this isn't a policy debate — it's a choice they have to make before year-end.

3:07 Farmers are going back from hemp to blackberries and corn
Tennessee farmer Lee Crabtree's farm used to grow mostly CBD-variety hemp, and the new state law makes selling those products illegal, so he's gone back to traditional seasonal crops like blackberries and corn. The family still has the industrial kitchen from its CBD food days; his wife Stacy now uses that big stainless-steel counter to cut grapes for chicken salad and sells it at a roadside farmers market. Lee says income is down, and if the traditional crops don't sell, he'll have to go find a job. This is what the ban looks like landing on one household.

5:08 The regulator's case: consumers don't know what they're drinking
Tennessee Republican Representative William Lamberth uses a drinks analogy: someone buying a Sprite expects a Sprite, not a beer; someone buying a beer expects a beer, not a tequila; someone buying a tequila expects not to get a Sprite. He says the goal is for consumers to know exactly what they're buying. But even farmers who agree with the logic worry the law overcorrects. The show also gives the other side: big companies are laying people off, and some are simply moving across state lines — Emily Schaeferich's company Burning Acre moved from Columbia, Tennessee, to North Carolina to keep growing, and she admits ripping up an entire retail, manufacturing and wholesale supply chain ‘does cost quite a bit of money’.

6:10 Moving to another state may be wasted effort
Hemp economist Beau Whitney calls the nationwide ban taking effect in December an ‘extinction-level event’. His mechanism: cannabis can only be grown in certain states, while hemp can be grown and shipped anywhere, so hemp businesses can build supersized capacity, push costs down and ship nationwide; cannabis, by contrast, needs a separate supply chain per state and can't get hemp's economies of scale. The result is that hemp-derived foods are far cheaper than their cannabis equivalents. So even in states where recreational cannabis is legal, consumers will feel the squeeze when they lose the cheap alternative.

7:13 The ban also takes out state tax revenue
The show singles out economies of scale to explain: the more of the same good you produce, the lower the unit cost, and the savings can be passed on to consumers. That also explains why hemp-derived foods are cheaper than cannabis products. But consumers aren't the only ones affected. For many state budgets, losing the hemp industry means losing a sizable source of tax revenue — in Tennessee alone, a $54 million budget hole. Beau Whitney also says it could put hundreds of thousands of jobs at risk.

7:13 The delay just moves it from November to December
The White House has urged Congress to delay or amend the ban, the Senate currently supports it, and the House voted earlier this month to delay it too. But those moves only push the effective date from November to December — a one-month delay. For companies that have already moved across state lines and rebuilt supply chains, a month changes nothing: they may have just moved the whole business only to find the industry destroyed in December.

8:14 Those staying behind switch to fiber hemp
Tennessee farmer Bill Corbin, in Springfield, is preparing the first fiber hemp crop for the French company Hemp-It; this kind of hemp is used for rope, packaging and auto parts. He says there isn't a single person in the industry who didn't know this day was coming, that he thinks the industry was unsustainable to begin with, and he agrees with legislators' efforts to suppress recreational use of hemp derivatives. But he worries about medical consumers: he himself is older and has arthritis, relies heavily on full-spectrum CBD, and the products left after the ban may not be strong enough for older people or those trying to avoid opioid painkillers.

item.title: The Bat Doesn't Know What It's Like to Be a Bat Either
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-pel-蝙蝠自己也不知道当蝙蝠是什么感觉/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-pel-蝙蝠自己也不知道当蝙蝠是什么感觉/
item.description: The bat argument rests on a private inner core that can never be reached; Dennett says that core doesn't exist, and that a bat isn't even a "what it's like" to itself.
item.content:encoded:
The bat argument rests on a private inner core that can never be reached; Dennett says that core doesn't exist, and that a bat isn't even a "what it's like" to itself.

The second half of episode 400, and listenable on its own. The first half is about theories of consciousness; the second half slides unexpectedly into animal ethics, and the four of them never do settle their disagreement.

1:07 A bat having an inner world is not the same as its being conscious
Christopher summarises Dennett's response: he flatly denies Nagel — we can talk about what it's like to be a bat in all sorts of ways (by first ruling out the things a bat doesn't do, for instance), and with enough information we eventually get there, because "what it's like to be a bat" just is the discriminative, dispositional states the bat has. Dylan supplies the step Dennett actually rejects: drawing on von Uexküll's Umwelt and Innenwelt (surrounding world and inner world), Dennett grants that the bat has an inner world, which is not crazy; what he won't accept is going straight from "has an inner world" to "therefore consciousness exists," and that latter step is exactly the one Nagel uses to prove consciousness exists. Our mode of access is heterophenomenology: treat the bat's behaviour and physiology as a text in need of interpretation.

5:37 Consciousness is not an all-or-nothing property
Christopher reads out a passage from Dennett: are language-less animals not conscious at all? Dennett says the question shouldn't be taken as a matter of course, because it presupposes "something we've had a hard time getting rid of" — that consciousness is an all-or-nothing property that splits the universe into two utterly different categories: things that have it and things that don't. That dichotomy is what Dennett wants to dismantle; what he wants is consciousness in degrees. Christopher then offers his own version: he doesn't want to accept property dualism, he wants to deny the hard problem, because subjectivity can perfectly well have a biological and evolutionary explanation — agency and subjectivity co-evolved; a physical process organising itself from the inside so that it "feels like something" is a real biological phenomenon.

12:57 The bat doesn't know what it's like to be a bat either
Seth pushes the argument to its extreme: it isn't "we don't know what it's like to be a bat," it's that there is no "what it's like to be a bat as seen from the bat's side" at all; the bat itself doesn't know either, because it lacks the machinery to string experiences into a narrative and give them names. Dylan immediately marks the cost of this inference: if anything with dynamic activity has its own experience, then atoms count too, and that's panpsychism. Christopher says you don't have to go as far as atoms, but concedes the direction really does sound like panpsychism — he'd rather use a threshold: you need a feedback loop of sensing and acting before you can talk about a new way of being.

14:35 Even plants have a perspective in some sense
Mark digs up a line from Dennett's book: the perspective of a conscious observer is a refined descendant of the original perspective of the first replicators, which "divided the world into good and bad" — on that account even plants have a perspective in this sense, and "perspective" becomes a metaphor. Christopher then offers gradualism: from sponges to mantis shrimp to humans, subjectivity accumulates layer by layer and gets thicker and thicker, with a fuzzy threshold in between. Dylan wants to nail the threshold down harder: you can't use "complex" as the criterion, since weather is a complex self-maintaining system too; the difference is that living things can replicate themselves and have a wholeness, so the only thing the Earth lacks is its own replication.

19:47 You are a bunch of things, not a soul
Mark finds Dennett's 1994 reply collection Get Real, which uses snakes as an example: a snake has no central representation of "mouse," it just responds to prey through three separate sensory systems. Dennett's point is that the perceptual system we take to be a single whole is really a pile of little homunculi each making its own discriminations; you are not an Aristotelian form, a soul, an organisation that runs you — we are all a bunch of things. Christopher objects: failure to integrate information processing doesn't mean there's no self — the two hemispheres of a split-brain patient are also separate, and we don't conclude from that that he has no self; the snake may still have a more ancient, minimal sense of boundary and evaluative experience.

27:39 Reducing experience to discrimination looks a lot like behaviourism
Christopher says he agrees with Dennett 99%, and is stuck on the 1%: when Dennett wants to reduce a person to dispositional states, saying that experiencing red is nothing over and above being able to discriminate red from non-red and being in that discriminative state, it sounds like behaviourism. Seth offers a defence: even if the substrate is just discriminative states, subjective experience, the self, is a composite stitched together out of memory, imagination, representation and symbolic language — it weaves scattered discriminative states into a story with descriptions, meanings and colour, and that story is me. Christopher agrees about the narrative self, but points out that the bat has no metacognitive capacity to construct such a self.

38:54 You can club an iguana, but not a rabbit
Mark says "everyone is a world" is a good moral fiction, but he doesn't know how to apply it to animals: Florida has too many iguanas, and he encourages people to go out and club them, which he says is completely fine and humane; swap in a rabbit and he won't accept it. Seth offers an evolutionary explanation: our feelings about animals domesticated over tens of thousands of years, wild animals and reptiles were never the same to begin with, and this doesn't conflict with the self being a narrative centre of gravity. Christopher anchors it in valence: animals are not reflex machines, they are situated perspectives that evaluate, and that is the reason they enter moral consideration — he says that after reading Lars Chittka's The Mind of a Bee, the way he deals with bees changed.

46:10 Take away caring and nothing of the pain is left
Mark turns to where Dennett talks specifically about pain: what is the functional relation of pain? If you take away caring about it and wanting to avoid it, take away everything else, and leave only the sensation of pain, then nothing is left — your not liking the pain is itself part of the pain. Mark says this is exactly Dennett's attitude to philosophical zombies: imagine someone biologically identical to you, with identical reactions and even identical internal relations, but the light of consciousness never came on — Dennett thinks this is so absurd that it's hard even to explain to scientists.

item.title: Beijing's Central Axis Is Not a Relic — It's a City Operating System Still Running
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-historyhit-北京中轴线不是古迹-是仍在运转的城市操作系统/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-historyhit-北京中轴线不是古迹-是仍在运转的城市操作系统/
item.description: The Ming rebuilt Beijing from a blueprint written two thousand years earlier, and the central axis still dictates the symmetry and growth of a city of twenty million — even the Olympic Bird's Nest sits on that line.
item.content:encoded:
The Ming rebuilt Beijing from a blueprint written two thousand years earlier, and the central axis still dictates the symmetry and growth of a city of twenty million — even the Olympic Bird's Nest sits on that line.

Medium information density, but its strength is restoring the central axis from tourist attraction to a planning logic still in force — suited to anyone interested in cities and organizational design.

7:13 A manual from two thousand years ago is still in use
When the Ming set out to rebuild the capital, they dug up a technical manual more than two thousand years old, the Kaogong Ji (“考工记”). It specified a city four to five kilometres on each side, three gates per side, the palace at the centre, an ancestral temple on one side, the court in front, the market behind, and a Temple of Heaven in the southern suburbs. The historian Jeremiah Jenik says the logic behind this layout was cosmic order: there is a fixed point in the sky, the North Star, so there should be a corresponding fixed point on earth, and the most fitting fixed point is the emperor himself — placing yourself in the palace at the exact centre of the city is placing yourself inside a cosmic order that revolves around you.

9:16 They actually built it to the drawing
The most astonishing thing is not that the Ming dared to use a blueprint over a thousand years old, but how closely they built to it. Overlay the Kaogong Ji drawing on the model at the Beijing Planning Exhibition Hall and the two almost coincide. So Beijing today is still a twenty-first-century city running around a fifteenth-century heart, and that heart follows principles laid down nearly two thousand years ago. Compare London, which grew organically along the Thames: Beijing had the blueprint first, then the city.

11:20 The central axis is a spine, and the city grew out of it
From north to south, the axis strings together the Bird's Nest, the Drum and Bell Towers, Jingshan, the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, and finally Yongdingmen at the southern end. The show likens it to a spine: everything is planned and expanded outward from this line. Running true north-south and aligned with the heavens, it has been Beijing's most distinctive feature for six hundred years, and it determines the shape of the city today.

12:22 The right to tell time is the right to rule
The Drum and Bell Towers were the timekeeping centre of the whole city, and the bell was said to carry twenty kilometres. From 1272 all the way to 1924 — the year the last Qing emperor left the Forbidden City — the time struck here was Beijing's official time. The drum was beaten one hundred and eight times every two hours; it was the first sound Beijingers heard in the morning and the last they heard at night. The show says it is almost as if the emperor were not merely marking time but claiming ownership of time itself.

15:32 Jingshan was piled up from the rubble of the previous dynasty
Jingshan is not a natural hill; it was built artificially by the Yongle Emperor according to feng shui principles. An ideal palace faces south, with water to the south — water that must bend and flow to bring qi and life — and a mountain to the north to block the evil qi coming from that direction and display authority. Beijing is too far from the Yan Mountains to the north, so the Ming used rubble from the old Mongol palaces and earth dug out of new canals to build a symbolic mountain inside the city.

18:52 The Forbidden City was a super-project of nationwide mobilization
Ten thousand logs were shipped from 1,800 kilometres to the southwest, golden bricks from Suzhou 1,100 kilometres to the south, 18 million bricks fired in all, and gold leaf brought from Nanjing. One million labourers plus more than 100,000 craftsmen built it in fifteen years. From the 1420s to the early twentieth century, twenty-four emperors lived here. Today it receives more than 15 million visitors a year, making it the most visited historic site on earth.

22:55 A nail-free timber structure can take a magnitude 9.5 quake
These buildings are almost entirely wood, and what lets them stand for centuries is the dougong (斗拱): the dou are the bearing blocks, the gong are inserted and interlock very tightly. Wood shrinks and warps, and this system lets it deform flexibly while keeping the overall structure intact; in an earthquake every small piece of wood can slide a little, without shearing the bearing blocks or popping screws. Scientists have calculated that this construction could withstand a magnitude 9.5 earthquake, the strongest ever recorded.

23:57 It was struck by lightning within a year of completion
The Forbidden City was not fireproof. Less than a year after it was completed in 1421, the three great halls burned to ashes after a lightning strike. Afterwards 308 bronze vats were installed to store water against the next fire. The detail makes the point: no matter how precise the planning, it cannot stop a single point of failure — you can only add redundancy after the fact.

item.title: Germany's CDU Falls Out of a State Parliament: The Era of the Centre Is Over
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-goodfight-德国基民盟跌出州议会-中间派时代已经结束/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-goodfight-德国基民盟跌出州议会-中间派时代已经结束/
item.description: The CDU won under 5% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, shut out of a state parliament for the first time since the Federal Republic was founded. Merz has lost his authority, and the populist far left and far right command an overwhelming majority among voters under 35.
item.content:encoded:
The CDU won under 5% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, shut out of a state parliament for the first time since the Federal Republic was founded. Merz has lost his authority, and the populist far left and far right command an overwhelming majority among voters under 35.

This is a piece of German domestic political commentary, not an interview. Information density is moderate, but it lays out the judgment that "populism has become the mainstream" very clearly — suited to anyone watching the direction of European politics.

0:00 The CDU is shut out of a state parliament for the first time
In the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state election, the CDU won under 5% of the vote and therefore holds no seats in that state parliament — the first time this has happened in the history of the Federal Republic. In the same election the AfD took roughly 38% of the vote, once again becoming the state's largest party. The author calls this the "final nail in the coffin" for Merz: he may hang on as chancellor for a few more weeks or months, but his authority has vanished, his capacity to shape the country is completely exhausted — in political language, "a dead man walking."

0:00 The CDU's decline came later than the SPD's but is just as fatal
The CDU is the most important party in postwar German history, governing the Federal Republic for 53 of the past 77 years, and from Adenauer to Kohl to Merkel it left its mark on every aspect of the country. The author notes that in the early 2000s everyone was talking about "the crisis of social democracy," as the SPD fell from over 40% support to record lows; in hindsight, the fate of the centre-left big party was only a leading indicator of a broader crisis of the entire political centre, and the CDU then walked the same road. The era of what Germans call the Volksparteien — catch-all parties capable of mobilising most of the vote — is effectively over.

0:00 The populists are not a fringe phenomenon but the most important political force
The author says this is the most-asked question of the past decade: "Will the populist wave last, or is it about to peak?" In the summer of 2016, when Trump became the Republican nominee and Britain voted for Brexit, the answer seemed obvious to him; now the answer is undeniable — the populists are here to stay. What looked abnormal a few years ago has, whether you like it or not, become the mainstream. Populist politicians now hold power in the United States, India, Turkey and many parts of the democratic world, and have a very high probability of taking office in France and Brazil in the coming months. Even where they remain in opposition, they are already strong enough to destroy any sense of business as usual.

0:00 The rise of one extremist party is feeding another
In the Berlin state election, Die Linke took 26% of the vote and emerged the big winner. The party descends from the SED, which ruled East Germany with an iron fist, and after reunification initially appealed mainly to older voters nostalgic for the security of the communist system; in recent years it has reinvented itself in the image of the global illiberal left, which the author considers roughly comparable to Zack Polanski's Greens in Britain or the more extreme parts of the DSA in the United States. During the campaign, some of the party's supporters were filmed chanting "Yalla, Yalla Intifada!"; on election night, the head of a notorious crime family visited the party's election party and cheerfully told the media he felt an affinity with it. The party's leader is now very likely to become the next mayor of Berlin, which would be the first time an SED successor has taken power in the capital.

0:00 Voters under 35 have swung to the two extremes
Another notable feature of the two elections is the age distribution. The SPD and CDU, which once dominated Germany's political landscape, draw most of their support from pensioners. Among voters under 35, Die Linke and the AfD hold unassailable majorities in both Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. From this the author concludes that an even larger tilt toward the extremes will come in the next few years. It also explains why the collapse of the centre is not a one-off election accident: the structure of the electorate itself is pushing the scales toward the two ends.

0:00 The left-wing coalition in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern is just an election accident
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, because a batch of other parties all failed to clear the 5% threshold for entering parliament, a broad left-wing coalition just barely won enough votes to govern. But the author stresses that this is an election accident unlikely to be repeated — a gap of a few thousand votes would leave the state completely ungovernable. This point is crucial: when centrist parties fall below the threshold, they don't just lose their own seats; they push the governability of the entire state to the edge of a cliff.

0:00 Don't surrender, and don't deny that the problem is real
The author explicitly rejects two responses. The first is to urge the centre to surrender: if the political centre can't hold, then moderates might as well defect to the extremists on "their own side." He thinks this is wrong — neither Die Linke nor the AfD can solve the real problems Germany faces, and despite their enormous differences they have conspicuous similarities, from their ambiguity toward Moscow to their persistent inability to purge antisemites from their ranks. The second is to keep denying reality: for a decade the centre has attributed the extremists' success to foreign interference, social media algorithms, some candidate's tactical blunder, or the stupidity, sexism or racism of voters. The author says these ways of blinding yourself to the facts in front of you may be comforting, but they are just as dangerous.

item.title: Going global: don't wait until you're big to go to Europe and America — go there first to get big
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-beiwanglu-出海别等做大了再去欧美-先去欧美才能做大/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-beiwanglu-出海别等做大了再去欧美-先去欧美才能做大/
item.description: Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and America once they're big, but it's exactly the reverse — you go there to become big. Get the region choice wrong and the later product 3.0 and channel pyramid won't stand up.
item.content:encoded:
Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and America once they're big, but it's exactly the reverse — you go there to become big. Get the region choice wrong and the later product 3.0 and channel pyramid won't stand up.

Wei Zhe compresses ten years of overseas investment experience into four choices, counterintuitive but each backed by cases and numbers, especially the second half on AI transforming organizations and pricing, which is the most information-dense.

1:30 The old cross-border mega-seller path is dead
Wei Zhe says the ‘cross-border mega-seller’ popular in Shenzhen is a distribution-style mindset, with dozens or hundreds of accounts; he has seen companies with over a thousand accounts and hundreds of thousands of SKUs. A decade ago these companies made money faster than other paths, and many investors loved them. But distribution-style companies are essentially traffic-style companies: the more stores, the more likely to get traffic. When platforms don't have enough goods, distribution isn't opposed; once goods are abundant, using distribution to grab traffic is bad money driving out good. More critically, three red lines: selling goods not as described harms consumers, fake orders harm other merchants, and inserting small cards to build private domains harms the platform. Amazon's flywheel places great importance on consumer experience, and these behaviors hit exactly that protective wall.

4:38 Four choices, region comes first
Wei Zhe says it's not just cross-border e-commerce; all of life is about choices being more important than effort. He gives four choices: region, channel, product category, and brand positioning. On region, he has always advocated seizing the European and American markets first, because of strong purchasing power, high internet penetration, and more importantly, the brand can build momentum. This isn't their invention; when Japanese and Korean brands went global, they all seized Europe and America. On category, they change their advice every three years: the first three years they supported products with universal appeal between China and abroad, where the domestic supply chain could sell overseas without modification, like Anker's power banks, which were almost identical except for voltage; the second three years they advised making overseas-exclusive products, because China's supply chain had gone global and universal products had no differentiation; the most recent three years is product 3.0 — electric, with chips, with algorithms.

12:29 It's not that you go to Europe and America after getting big; you get big by going there
Many companies tell Wei Zhe, ‘I'll go to Europe and America when I'm big,’ and he says it's exactly the reverse: you go to Europe and America to become big. He gives the example of Cupshe, a swimwear company: a husband and wife, with $50,000 of inventory, and their first stop was the US. $50,000 is the goods for sale, actually very little, so there's no minimum threshold. He recently looked at AI smart hardware, starting from Kickstarter crowdfunding with a thousand or ten thousand products, even taking pre-orders before placing orders, with no capital — that's also a great way to test the waters. He even advises big companies entering the European and American markets to learn from small startups. They always say the needle must be fine enough to pierce; both big and small companies should first do the four singles well: single market, single category, single channel, single brand.

20:36 After AI, good companies don't just find demand, they create it
Wei Zhe says with AI, excellent companies don't look for demand, they should lead demand and create demand. He gives the example of a Chinese company making astronomical telescopes: originally not electric, they electrified it, added chips and algorithms; the algorithm is actually simple, with GPS positioning, and the map of the universe's movements is regular. He wasn't an astronomy enthusiast but would buy one; at home in Silicon Valley, with one tap, it automatically aligns to Orion for you, tells you the best viewing is at 3 a.m., you set it and go to sleep, and the next day it takes the photos for you. This lets everyone become a good astronomy enthusiast. Another example: a cross-border class student making curtains, which didn't sell well in the US after being electrified because American electricians are expensive, so he put solar panels on the window, turning electric curtains that need an electrician into DIY ones; revenue went from one or two hundred million to four or five hundred million, with profit of one or two hundred million.

24:48 In the AI era, still using subscription fees means you're behind
Wei Zhe says in the AI era, if you still think in terms of subscription fees, you're behind again; they are all advising companies to do back-end charging, software charging, called tokenized. A monthly subscription fee is the dumbest way, a bit like advertising charging by time instead of by usage. This time AI has brought out the most ideal charging model in all of human education: paying according to your usage of AI software, services, or content. He gives an example: Bessie, if you take two weeks off this month, isn't subscribing for a month a waste of two weeks? They suggest that AI-transformed hardware should be charged like AI, not the old SaaS model of $9.9 per month. An AI reading platform he looked at charges by how many articles you read, and nothing if you don't read; the same with smart bike trainers: after topping up, one dollar per ride, two dollars for two hours.

27:28 Adding AI is more promising than AI plus
Wei Zhe has a view called AI plus or plus AI; he reverses the phrase and says he's more optimistic about plus AI rather than today's AI plus. The difference: plus AI is taking hardware humans have already accepted and making it AI; rather than creating a previously unseen hardware because of AI. It's very hard for humans to accept a brand-new hardware. For example, Oura makes rings, because you first accepted rings; some things that hang a camera under your neck are harder for me, I haven't accepted that hardware. So they are very optimistic about adding AI to already-accepted hardware. They invested in a capacitive stylus that is number one globally, because everyone already writes on a Pad, it doesn't add an extra pen, it just makes your pen AI. He also especially wants to transform one of the top fitness equipment companies going global, replacing the fitness coach on the screen with AI-generated ones — you want a male, it's male; you want a Black person, it's Black; install two cameras and you get AI-guided fitness.

29:43 Channels aren't flat; they're a pyramid
Wei Zhe says channels aren't multiple channels multiple paths, each channel parallel or even competing; excellent brands all have a channel pyramid. Like luxury brands and traditional brands, there must be different channel strategies, pricing strategies, and which channel new products launch in first. What is a light-goods channel, what is the main waist volume channel — the pyramid design differs by category and brand. He gives Anker: making power bank mecha seems a bit low, to enter the consumer electronics high ground of Soundcore earphones you have to get into Apple flagship stores; whether it really sells a lot isn't important, but it can transform the brand, Apple is the pyramid's peak. Pop Mart must open on London's Oxford Street, even if it doesn't make money, how much can it lose, but it must be propped up there. He says some companies treat Temu and AliExpress as parallel channels to sell goods, which definitely won't work; AliExpress is a light-goods channel, when Amazon delists you, you dump it there, you can't sell on Amazon and here too, consumers get confused.

36:14 R&D is 1, marketing is 0
Wei Zhe says he really dislikes spending heavily on marketing. Many Chinese brands going global or cross-border e-commerce are willing to add 2% of revenue to marketing expenses, but consumers don't get it. He says, do you dare to add 2% of revenue to R&D expenses? He has met many bosses with 1 billion or 2 billion scale; a 1 billion boss says 20 million for R&D, I don't know what for. He says, see, there's the problem, you don't know what for. Your 2% on marketing makes the platform happy, consumers don't get it; but 2% into R&D, consumers get it. He has always firmly believed good products speak for themselves, marketing is just — your R&D is 1, marketing is 0; if you have something good you can amplify it, if you don't have that 1, never put many 0s. He gives three judgment signals: first, dare to find a benchmark company, definitely a mid-to-upper brand, and you crush it by doubling performance; second, you sell at the same high price as it; third, you sell online and hit offline channels to come to you.

item.title: The AI office hype hasn't cleared, and the personal Agent war has already begun | Breaking down Town, Instinct, Grok Bot and Muse
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-luanfanshu-10万用户估值100亿-个人agent的估值跑在产品前面/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-luanfanshu-10万用户估值100亿-个人agent的估值跑在产品前面/
item.description: Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and its product isn't officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50 million to $10 billion in half a year — in this round of personal Agent heat, capital grabbing a ticket matters more than real demand.
item.content:encoded:
Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and its product isn't officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50 million to $10 billion in half a year — in this round of personal Agent heat, capital grabbing a ticket matters more than real demand.

Four frontline product people break down four routes — Town, Instinct, Grok Bot, Muse — and also explain why that batch of products like Xiaolongxia became martyrs. Information density is high, but the second half is worth more.

0:00 100,000 users prop up a $10 billion valuation
Instinct only began small-scale invite testing in February this year, and by the end of August it still hadn't reached 100,000 users, yet its valuation went from $50 million at the start of the year to $500 million in August, $2.5 billion at the end of August, and this month the new round being quoted in the market has already reached $10 billion, with Sequoia and Benchmark both in talks to lead. The founder is a 23-year-old unknown with no big-company experience, no technical patents, no industry background. Pan Luan (潘乱) put it bluntly: what capital is buying is neither the founder nor the product, it's the story of the next OpenAI, and it can pay the price of the next-generation personal operating system to grab a ticket.

15:16 The line between tool and person is initiative
The biggest difference between this wave of Agents and the last is that it is no longer another tool, but a person. Two differences between a person and a tool: first, long-term understanding — a tool needs the context explained again every time, while a person understands what kind of person you are like a friend or colleague; second, initiative — in Manus, setting up an automated task still depends on a prompt, on you spelling out the rules and intent, and that isn't initiative. Real initiative is subjective agency — like the colleague who understands your goal in doing something and proactively comes over to say, "I have a plan, should we discuss it?"

18:09 Office Agents organise by project, personal Agents organise by person
The most core difference is the dimension along which context is built. Cloud Code builds context along a mission or project dimension, and switching to the next project means starting over; this wave of personal agents builds context centred on you as a person, knowing your profile, preferences and past history. Open Codex or Manus and the list on the left is all the tasks and projects you've sent out; open Grok Bot and beside you are AI companions you can drive together. In personal scenarios people care less about model capability and the harness layer, because individuals don't have that many complex tasks; office Agents are the ones that care a lot about task completion rate.

30:28 Town first trades email for the user's right to delegate
