The four products are trying to solve the same problem, just with different approaches. Town has a mobile client, but 70% of its data traffic is on PC; it focuses on the email scenario, solving one high-frequency scenario well before expanding. It understands which emails you send and receive often, auto-archives, learns your writing style, drafts replies for you, and sends automatically after you confirm. It goes deeper in the email scenario than any other agent, and overseas it has already achieved fairly viral spread, spreading especially well in school-type scenarios. In one sentence: use a high-frequency scenario to build user trust, and acquire the user's ultimate right to delegate bit by bit.

39:33 Poke didn't break out, and it wasn't a technical limit
Poke and Instinct are both agents that live inside IM and don't make a standalone app, but Poke didn't break out. Suki believes it wasn't a technical limit — Browser Use was already very mature by the end of last year, and Poke could absolutely have done it at the time; the difference was team strategy: Instinct went deeper in the agent direction, taking the full-delegation route, able to connect to credit cards, screen and microphone, booking flights and buying things for you — things users hadn't seen before, which produced viral spread; Poke put its energy into content push accuracy, taking the proactive-push route, with email notifications arriving even earlier than the inbox itself, but it didn't take the step of "getting things done for you".

42:39 A cloud Agent has to handle three environments
Mark says doing a cloud agent was a painful lesson: a local agent and a cloud agent are completely different things. To do personal AI you have to be usable anytime, anywhere — you can't be unreachable just because the computer screen is off. The cloud has to handle three environments — the user's device, the cloud service, and the agent's execution environment — and task state, task interruption and recovery, and context passing between the three are very complex systems. They started in February, and just getting the agent to run stably on the cloud took at least two months; setting aside detours, polishing a sincere piece of work takes at least three to four months.

50:39 Hiring an assistant and being a middleman are two different businesses
Town started out doing corporate tax filing, and after pivoting it leans more toward enterprise scenarios; the relationship is more like you paying to hire a personal assistant, which naturally filters for people willing to pay, with a typical profile of white-collar workers who are extremely busy and have no time or energy. Muse is more like a middleman, shopping guide or broker: although it has a paid subscription, the main projected revenue source is still commission from matchmaking transactions, leaning toward mass users and blending into everyday WhatsApp chats. Two completely different logics, cutting different scenarios and filtering out different users.

1:14:07 For an Agent, the saved folder may be noise
The story Zuckerberg told when launching Muse was extracting what you like to eat from Instagram-saved ingredients, generating a shopping list, adjusting the menu by dinner party size and dietary restrictions, then completing the shopping and relationship maintenance — turning years of interest profile into money, going from a discovery platform to a decision-and-transaction platform. But Suki suspects this is to save face for the free business narrative: helping users close transactions is absolutely not among the top scenarios users want to solve; users more want to solve the annoying things they don't want to do themselves. There isn't that much high-quality context in saved folders; the truly high-quality context comes more from offline, IM and email, and Douyin and Instagram saves may themselves be noise to an agent.

item.title: Ten Years of Parenting Taught Me: When Your Kid Won't Listen, the Problem Isn't Your Kid
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-parentmojo-育儿十年才懂-孩子不听话时-问题不在孩子身上/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-parentmojo-育儿十年才懂-孩子不听话时-问题不在孩子身上/
item.description: On the podcast's tenth anniversary, the host revisits ten parenting beliefs she once held as certain — from forcing her daughter to take medicine to treating an expert's framework as gospel — each one learned first in a book, then relearned in a real conflict.
item.content:encoded:
On the podcast's tenth anniversary, the host revisits ten parenting beliefs she once held as certain — from forcing her daughter to take medicine to treating an expert's framework as gospel — each one learned first in a book, then relearned in a real conflict.

For parents who want to interrogate their own parenting methodology. Medium information density, heavy on personal narrative, but the ten reflections are clearly structured, and the back half — on "the village" and the couple relationship — is more valuable than the front half.

6:00 Forcing the medicine won the behavior and lost the relationship
The host recalls her three-year-old daughter refusing antibiotics; she held her down and forced the medicine in, and her daughter threw most of it back up. That night her husband Alvin stayed with their daughter in the bathroom for an hour, calmly saying the whole time, "I'm willing to do anything, but we're not leaving until we figure this out." In the end the daughter finished the whole course herself, with small sips of medicine, small sips of water, and a small piece of chocolate to take the taste away. The host says the difference wasn't that her husband was more patient — it's that he wasn't solving a behavior, he was understanding what would actually help the child do this thing. What the child needed was autonomy over the process, and to feel that she and her parent were on the same team, rather than being held down to do something.

9:19 The authoritative parenting framework rests on 146 white kids
The host says she accepted uncritically early on that "authoritative is the best parenting style," because every blog and every study said so. It wasn't until she did the episode on corporal punishment that she found a paper co-authored by Diana Baumrind defending parents' ability to spank their children, and started digging. She found that this framework — cited more than 26,000 times, and which has defined sixty years of parenting research — was originally based on just 146 white, middle-class preschoolers in the town where Baumrind lived. She calls this evidence of her own insufficient critical thinking, and says she now asks at the macro level, "Does this theory make sense?" and at the micro level, "Does it fit this specific child in front of me?"

17:41 Not punishing your kid doesn't mean being ruled by your kid
The host says she once believed that without punishment and consequences a child would run wild — she even remembers standing in the shower when her daughter was four months old thinking, "How do I discipline her without becoming a mean mom?" Clinical psychologist Dr. Houri Parsi admitted in the membership community that she too had treated "obedience" as the goal, and that every tooth-brushing was a battle. Once, recording for the host to see, she deliberately used no threats, no punishment and no rewards, and simply asked her two-year-old son, "Why don't you want to brush your teeth?" He couldn't put it into words — he just called out "Mama" and buried his head in her chest. She realized what he wanted was time alone with her. She put the toilet lid down, sat down, held her son, and they sang a song together, and he brushed his teeth himself, the whole thing in under five minutes.

21:31 "I need you to take out the trash" is not a need
The host says that looking back, she didn't understand what a "need" was — she thought saying "I need you to take out the trash" to her husband was a perfectly logical sentence. Before their daughter was born the two of them almost never argued: mountain biking in summer, skiing in winter, because the ad agency they worked for represented resorts and paid them in vouchers. Everything changed after their daughter was born: during his three weeks of paternity leave her husband would fetch her anything she wanted, and the rest of the time he was training for a hundred-mile ride and watching the Tour de France. She says it was learning that she had needs for "collaboration, partnership, and having her effort seen" that actually pried open the problems between them; before that she was carrying a large amount of resentment inside her with no idea how to handle it.

24:01 When you're triggered, the problem isn't the person who interrupted you
The host says her biggest trigger is being interrupted — the moment her husband interrupts her she flies into a rage, most recently over how much postage a package needed. She always assumed the cause was simply that her husband interrupted her, and that if he stopped, everything would be fine. Recording in July 2018 with intergenerational trauma expert Dr. Rebecca Babcock-Fenerci, she traced it on the spot to her own father, a special education teacher who would treat sixteen-year-olds like ten-year-olds and who, for a stretch, lectured her every night. Later, in the car, she interrupted her daughter, and her daughter said, "Don't interrupt me, Mama," and her husband looked at her and said, "She is you." She says that was the moment she realized it had never just been about the two people in the room, and out of it she developed the "Tame Your Triggers" course, which grew from a one-month module to ten weeks.

30:27 The handmade book she made while pregnant was full of expectations for her child
The host describes a book she made while pregnant: three covers, one in the middle and one on each side, opening in both directions, brown book cloth with a beige spine, the word "me" cut out of the board on one cover and "you" embossed on the other when you flipped it over — the concept being "you came out of me." On the "me" side she wrote her own feelings and thoughts; on the "you" side she wrote to the not-yet-met Carys. She reads out the earliest batch of "expectations for you": I hope you're smart, or at least average; I hope you're the kind of child who shakes hands with people instead of hiding behind my legs; I hope you like both roughhousing and pretty things; I hope you don't cry all the time; I hope that when you fall you pick yourself up and say "I'm okay." She says looking back, the biggest mistake was not knowing how to simply be with a person and let them be their whole self and witness that, without carrying ideas about how they should be.

33:14 Kohn's principle two: reconsider your demands first
The host says she once thought she'd play the role of "enforcer" — she even wrote "I hope you can love me the way I love him" on her pregnancy expectations list. She says RIE loosened the soil for her, but what actually planted the seed was Alfie Kohn's Unconditional Parenting. She shares a few of its principles: principle two is to reconsider your demands — "maybe when a child won't do what you ask, the problem isn't the child, it's what you're asking"; principle five is to change how you look, not just how you act — when you see your child doing the thing you asked them not to do, your first reaction should be curiosity about what they're struggling with, not how to make them stop; principle ten is to "attribute to your child the best motive consistent with the observed facts," and she says when she quotes it she changes the ending to "consistent with the observed behavior," because "there are no facts, only what we observe."

39:07 The couple relationship isn't a different subject, it's the same one
The host says she long believed the couple relationship and the parent-child relationship were completely different things — when she started the parenting membership eight years ago she asked Dr. Laura Froyen to write the co-parenting module, because she had no idea how to handle a partner relationship. She says her parenting shift toward collaboration was relatively easy, because she had no ten-year-old habits with her daughter; but she and Alvin had been together ten years and had never learned how to disagree, because they spent most of that time doing hobbies they loved, and she didn't mind doing most of the housework. It wasn't until she did Gottman training that she realized this was almost the same work she'd been doing with her child all these years — while also believing the Gottman method itself has a few key flaws. She recruited couples from the membership to record real arguments and used modified tools; one couple, where the husband had refused to discuss a toxic issue, became willing to talk after his wife listened for ten minutes with a genuine intent to understand him, and they reached an agreement to move forward in that same session.

item.title: NPR's comment section was mistaken for bots — it was actually a group of middle schoolers
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-tal-npr-评论区被当成机器人-其实是一群初中生/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-tal-npr-评论区被当成机器人-其实是一群初中生/
item.description: NPR staff saw a flood of gibberish in the comments and their first instinct was bots, so they reported it; a younger colleague recognized it as kids whose parents had blocked social media, using a Spotify comment section as a group chat.
item.content:encoded:
NPR staff saw a flood of gibberish in the comments and their first instinct was bots, so they reported it; a younger colleague recognized it as kids whose parents had blocked social media, using a Spotify comment section as a group chat.

Four independent stories, medium information density, but the generational misjudgment details in the first story and the mother-daughter conversation about braiding in the third are both worth hearing.

1:01 The gibberish comments aren't bots, they're kids
Dave Blanchard saw a sudden flood of incomprehensible messages in the Wild Card comment section on Spotify, and his first instinct was bots, so he reported them to Spotify and had the posts deleted. But Hannah Chin, a colleague at NPR ten years younger, opened the screenshots and immediately reached the opposite conclusion: these are kids. Her evidence was the display names full of emoji that require a special character generator to type, the cartoon avatars she'd never seen before, and the back-and-forth short sentences with piles of exclamation marks. Dave wasn't buying it at first, and replied, "That's an interesting theory."

6:05 Using playlists as a group-chat doorway
Hannah kept digging and found how the kids operated: one kid creates a public playlist called Let's Chat Here or New Chat with just one podcast episode in it; other kids see the playlist, click into that episode, and chat in the comments. They also post Google Forms as little quizzes, writing "only cool people can fill this out." Hannah said bots don't go post Google Forms, but Gen Alpha does, the same way her own generation made UQuiz or BuzzFeed personality quizzes. That's the detail that finally convinced Dave.

8:06 They picked NPR because the comments were empty
The show reached out to several commenters, and only one, a 14-year-old girl named Ella, agreed to be interviewed; she did the interview from the car while her father drove. Ella said the core of the group is about 20 kids, many of them in drama club, mostly girls, with strict parents who won't let them use regular social media. They first chatted in the comment section of a podcast that played TikTok videos; after that podcast got shut down, the kids started using playlists to relocate. Asked why they chose NPR shows, Ella said: we look for podcasts that don't have many comments, so we don't get mixed up in other people's comments.

11:08 Dave needed a generational translator
After learning the truth, Dave said he felt guilty for reporting them, and also felt old. He said, "I literally needed Hannah to be my generational translator," and that this made him acutely aware of his age and how out of date he was. Ella, for her part, said she's sure that one day she'll be just as baffled as Dave. The show puts this segment at the top, as the entry point to the whole episode's theme of "intergenerational space travel."

25:35 The wedding toast was a poem nobody heard
At 18, Courtney read a poem she wrote at her mother's second wedding, and her mother held it against her for thirty years. The poem opens with the mother walking in habitual darkness, every breath like her last; the middle has the mother standing by the counter smoking; but the ending turns to "you found roots, you found a soul worth worshipping." The mother said that on the wedding day she only heard the negative first half and never heard the kindness at the end; rereading it, Courtney admitted that presenting a bride with such a dark picture on her wedding day would indeed make it impossible to hear the good part.

31:52 The body knew the marriage was wrong first
Two days after the wedding, the 49-year-old mother suffered a massive stroke. Courtney offers a theory: her mother's body, not her mind, had known all along that the marriage was a mistake. The mother agreed, saying she knew when she was buying the wedding dress, that she wasn't all that happy then, that she "anticipated this awfulness ahead of time," sensing it in every fiber. This exchange turns all the earlier arguing about the wedding toast into a question about why her mother didn't listen to her intuition back then.

39:05 Only kicking out the stepfather repaired mother and daughter
Last October, the mother fell in the kitchen Mr. X designed and broke her back; Mr. X was too drunk to help, and only handed her the phone hours later so she could call an ambulance herself. The mother was hospitalized for months and gave Courtney power of attorney to go to court and have Mr. X removed. Courtney said it was the hardest thing she's ever done, but they won. The mother said it was precisely because Courtney spent so much time here for that, that she realized how much her daughter cared about her. Mr. X drove them apart, and getting rid of him pulled them back together.

55:41 The mother says braiding shouldn't be the doorway to toughness
Myra Flynn locks horns with her six-year-old daughter Avalon every morning over braiding, and she blurted out "sometimes what we need isn't comfortable," then immediately realized those were her own mother's words. She called her mother, Martha Mathis, expecting support, but her mother said: braiding shouldn't be used as a doorway to make a child tough, because it carries too many racial and gender meanings; and besides, six-year-old Avalon is already the toughest little girl there is. Her mother's advice was to let Avalon handle a small section of hair herself, because "she'll be gentle with herself."

item.title: Robots Are Still at GPT-1, and the Real Signal Is Success Rate, Not Loss
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-crossing-机器人还在-gpt-1-阶段-真正的信号是成功率不是-loss/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-crossing-机器人还在-gpt-1-阶段-真正的信号是成功率不是-loss/
item.description: The Scaling Law signal for embodied intelligence has already appeared, but we're measuring the wrong metric: low loss does not mean high success rate, and fitting the 17 steps that never touch the object is meaningless.
item.content:encoded:
The Scaling Law signal for embodied intelligence has already appeared, but we're measuring the wrong metric: low loss does not mean high success rate, and fitting the 17 steps that never touch the object is meaningless.

Xu Mengdi (徐梦迪), assistant professor at Tsinghua's Institute for Interdisciplinary Information Sciences, on data, world models and In-Context Learning for embodied intelligence. The middle and later sections on the data loop and the loss trap are the most valuable.

12:15 Pretraining is not everything; adaptation is what matters
Xu Mengdi's CMU best doctoral thesis is called Building Adaptable Generalist Robots, and its core claim is: pretraining is extremely useful, but you cannot hope a robot will succeed 100% of the time on pretraining alone. The defining feature of the open world is that tasks keep changing — at home there are 20 objects today, a week later 30 of different kinds, and people's preferences change too. So the robot must be able to adapt to change in its deployment environment and improve itself. She explored two paths: In-Context Learning and test-time training; the latter changes only 0.5% of the adapter parameters, but change too much and it forgets the pretrained knowledge.

19:22 Why adaptation only became important now
Humans generalize well for two reasons: extremely strong priors, and learning things very fast. The mainstream approach until now has been to scale data and models so that multi-task and instruction-following abilities get stronger — essentially giving the model a strong enough prior first. But Xu Mengdi points out this does not mean adaptation is unimportant — it is just that people only recently realized it. And adaptation places demands on the base model: you don't want the robot's self-learning process in a real setting to be terrifying, like smashing a cup. So starting from pretraining is reasonable.

49:46 Low loss does not equal high success rate
This is the most counterintuitive technical judgment in the whole piece. There is a very tricky point in robotics: loss is not directly tied to success rate. Loss can be very low while the final success rate is not necessarily low — there will be a lot of oscillation. Her example: a task might take 20 steps in total, and the first 17 steps involve no contact with the object. Even if those 17 steps fit extremely well, if step 18, when contact actually happens, has a relatively large error, the task fails easily. This is an imbalance in the time sequence. So a Scaling Law that actually means something should be: as data gradually increases and the model gradually grows, success rate on unseen tasks gradually rises.

50:47 Robots are still at the GPT-1 moment
Today's mainstream embodied models are still ‘pretraining + fine-tuning on the target domain’, which can be compared to the GPT-1 stage of language models — GPT-1 itself also needed targeted post-training to solve the corresponding tasks. What Xu Mengdi really wants to achieve is the GPT-3 moment: giving the model task information through ICL, through prompting, with no fine-tuning needed, telling the model what to do purely through context. That way the weight of fine-tuning becomes much weaker, it scales more easily to more scenarios and more tasks, and ordinary people can use it too.

58:49 The data loop is a chicken-and-egg problem
The hardest point is whether you can give the model a stable data loop. That requires putting the robot into an end-user home or service scenario, having a suitable mentor to teach it, and the robot must show obvious progress after being taught for half an hour — only then will end users be willing to use it, and only then can the data loop start turning. But there is a chicken-and-egg problem here: the base model needs to be good enough and learn fast enough, yet the model also needs to get into the scenario first so users start using it, in order to draw out that base capability. So whether the data loop can be made to work is the riskiest point of all.

1:03:52 Data is defined by working backward from model capability
Data itself gets fed to the model, but the definition of data is not conjured out of thin air — it is defined by the model's capabilities. When people define data, what they are actually doing is: figuring out what capabilities the model needs, and working backward to how the data should be collected. For example, if you need smoother motion, the data should be of the smooth type; if you need fail-recovery ability, the data should be collected with failures and corrections in it. And right now people's definition of model capability is still fairly vague, so the data requirements are vague too.

1:05:54 Each of the four data types has its own place
Xu Mengdi's position is that of a fusionist, because different data teaches the model different things. Teleoperation data is closest to the robot body itself, suited to the post-training stage, making the model more directly relevant to the target domain. Simulation data easily produces position generalization and texture generalization, making the model more robust to visual change, and suits the front end of pretraining or mid-training. UMI data sits in the middle, more like robot data but cheaper to collect. Human data is the cheapest, can be spread widely across different scenarios, and what it teaches is scene variation and task-relevant information, less tied to the specific shape of the morphology.

1:19:02 AI-written papers are obvious at a glance
Robotics papers have recently been doubling in number, and Xu Mengdi's way of coping is to scroll through articles promoted by the researchers she follows, because the author list itself has already done a layer of filtering. She can clearly see that some articles have a very large AI-written component. Her judgment: AI-written articles may pass review and actually get into some conferences, but overall the quality still won't be higher than human-written ones, because they look familiar while in fact many arguments are full of holes and there isn't much content. Once she finds out a paper was written by AI, her interest in it is discounted.

item.title: The woman who killed Marat, and why the court wouldn't believe she acted alone
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-restishistory-刺杀马拉的女人-为什么法庭不信她独自行动/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-restishistory-刺杀马拉的女人-为什么法庭不信她独自行动/
item.description: Corday had her declaration written before the assassination, and after her arrest she insisted she acted alone — yet the revolutionary tribunal kept pressing her on the "chain of conspiracy." They could not imagine that provincials thought Marat a monster.
item.content:encoded:
Corday had her declaration written before the assassination, and after her arrest she insisted she acted alone — yet the revolutionary tribunal kept pressing her on the "chain of conspiracy." They could not imagine that provincials thought Marat a monster.

High information density: it strings the institutional origins of the Terror, paper-money inflation and the Vendée war into a single causal chain, and the assassination detail in the back half is especially valuable.

0:00 The assassination declaration was written before the act
When Corday was arrested she was carrying a declaration titled "To the Friends of Law and Peace in France." In it she named Marat "the most vile of scoundrels," said he "has been condemned by the universe, and is therefore outside the law," and called on the French to "rise up. Strike. Strike." This text was not a post-hoc defence — it was written before the act. What she wanted was not escape, but to turn her own death into a rallying point.

9:30 Marat was the first modern populist
Keith Michael Baker's new biography positions Marat as the first modern populist. His recipe included: constantly invoking the capital-P "People," and claiming the people were at every moment in danger of being betrayed by appeasers and traitors; an obsession with conspiracy theory, openly stating that his goal was to keep his readers "perpetually on their guard," lest they be dragged into the abyss by royalists, priests and their ilk. The show points out that this "wake up, sheep" language is used by both left and right today.

21:57 Paper-money inflation pushed the poor into the streets
In early 1793 France had suffered years of poor harvests, the national grain market collapsed, and the government had no money to fight its wars, so it printed paper money — the assignat — with roughly four billion in circulation. This triggered violent inflation, bread and sugar prices soared, there were protests in the market almost daily, and women's marches appeared in the streets of Paris. The show stresses: these were exactly the same conditions that had set off the Revolution and the storming of the Bastille, and the poor would think, "the Revolution happened, yet life hasn't improved — so someone must be scheming."

32:13 The commander-in-chief's defection confirmed the conspiracy theories
On 8 March 1793 the Austrians counter-attacked and routed Dumouriez at Neerwinden; he was forced to withdraw from Belgium and Holland. He wanted to march on Paris and become a military dictator in the manner of Sulla, and asked his officers, "Shall we march on Paris?" They said no. On 5 April he rode over to the Austrian lines, taking a number of senior officers with him, including the future King of France, Louis Philippe. One volunteer wrote to his mother: "Who can we trust now?"

38:27 The Terror machine was improvised, not planned
The show stresses that the key institutions of the Terror had no blueprint and no plan — they were built as they went, and only in hindsight did they assemble into a machine, and many of those who helped build it were eventually swallowed by it. On 10 March the Revolutionary Tribunal was established to try political crimes, with death sentences to be carried out within 24 hours and no right of appeal; it sat in the Palais de Justice in Paris, and its cellars were the existing Conciergerie prison. Danton said: "Let us be terrible, so that the people need not be."

42:37 The Girondins used a new rule to strike at Marat, and it backfired
Having just abolished parliamentary immunity, the Girondins took advantage of the many deputies away on missions to the provinces and, on 14 April, brought an indictment against Marat, accusing him of inciting insurrection. Marat went into hiding for three days, then found that street opinion in Paris was on his side and simply turned himself in for trial. On 24 April the court convened in the Palais de Justice; the prosecutor, Fuquietanville, was a Montagnard sympathiser and let Marat deliver a long speech in his own defence. The ten-man jury acquitted him within a few hours, and Marat was carried back to the National Convention by some 800 people, crowned with roses, with cries of "vive la république, vive Marat." For the Girondins it was a total humiliation.

1:04:31 Corday buys a knife: a 15-centimetre black-handled kitchen knife
At around eight in the morning on 13 July, Charlotte Corday left her hotel, walked to the arcades of the Palais-Royal, bought a newspaper (which said the Convention would probably sentence the imprisoned Girondin deputies to death), and bought a black Paris hat with a green ribbon, replacing the white Norman-style hat that marked her out. She went into a cutler's shop called Le Coutelier Badin and bought a kitchen knife with a black handle and a blade about 15 centimetres long. Between 11:30 a.m. and noon she took a carriage to Marat's house on the rue des Cordeliers, but she had no appointment and was turned away by Marat's sister-in-law.

1:10:51 The court would not believe a woman could act alone
Corday was arrested on the spot, and one of her interrogators was Jean-Baptiste Drouet, the postmaster who had recognised Louis XVI's flight at Varennes. From the start she said she had acted alone. But the revolutionary tribunal repeatedly interrogated her about the "chain of conspiracy," convinced she must be part of a Girondin plot. The interrogator Montané said: that is impossible, because you say Marat was the source of all France's ills, yet Marat was precisely the man who never stopped exposing traitors and conspirators — so someone must have lied to you. Corday replied: you are mad; only in Paris do people see Marat, in the other provinces he is taken for a monster. The court could not imagine that provincials would think Marat a bad man.

item.title: Intel's Optane Died Because 3D NAND Was Too Cheap, Not Because the Tech Was Bad
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-asianometry-intel-的-optane-死于-3d-nand-太便宜-不是技术不行/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-asianometry-intel-的-optane-死于-3d-nand-太便宜-不是技术不行/
item.description: Phase-change memory was worked on from 1970 to 2022, and every time it got squeezed out by cheaper flash. 3D XPoint was stuck between NAND and DRAM, worse than both, and in the end even Intel gave up on it.
item.content:encoded:
Phase-change memory was worked on from 1970 to 2022, and every time it got squeezed out by cheaper flash. 3D XPoint was stuck between NAND and DRAM, worse than both, and in the end even Intel gave up on it.

A complete history of a storage technology's failure, from RMM in 1970 to the shutdown of Optane in 2022. Medium information density; the back half on data-center deployment and Micron's exit is the most valuable part.

3:07 The physics of phase-change storage is what makes it slow
Phase-change storage writes data by switching a material between its crystalline and amorphous states: the crystalline state has low resistance, the amorphous state high resistance, and the two differ by three to four orders of magnitude. Melting the material and quenching it into the amorphous state is called RESET; the reverse is called SET. SET either melts the material into a liquid and lets it cool slowly into a crystal, or heats it to a temperature high enough to convert it directly to crystalline without melting. The author points out that SET is often the speed bottleneck for PCM. This physical mechanism has not changed since Stanford Ovshinsky discovered the phase-change behavior of chalcogenide compounds in the 1960s.

4:13 Intel built phase-change memory in 1970, then forgot about it
In 1970, RG Neale and DL Nelson of Energy Conversion Devices and Intel's Gordon Moore published an article in Electronics magazine announcing "Read-Mostly Memory," positioned between RAM and ROM, for storing data that programs read often but rarely change. Each cell was a silicon diode plus a layer of phase-change material; Intel supplied the silicon substrate, ECD supplied the material. But in 1970 the minimum feature size was only 10 microns, power consumption was high, SET took milliseconds, and endurance was low. DRAM capacity was growing, EPROM arrived, and RMM disappeared. Years later someone asked the 79-year-old Moore about the article, and he said he had no memory of it at all.

9:25 Numonyx treated PCM as its only shot at a comeback
The rise of NAND sent NOR flash into a long decline, and in 2007 global NOR sales fell 9% year over year. Intel merged its NOR business with STMicroelectronics' flash business, forming the Swiss company Numonyx in 2008, with an investment from Francisco Partners and a bank loan. NOR had none of NAND's growth prospects, so Numonyx could only bet on PCM — PCM combined NOR's fast random reads with NAND's high-capacity storage, and in theory could replace both. In February 2008 Intel announced delivery of its first PCM prototype, Alverstone, at 128 megabit and 90 nanometers.

13:33 Mobile PCM was swept away in one wave by 3D NAND
PCM's entry strategy was to attack the mobile market, replacing the NOR flash that stores boot code while also storing data. In 2009 Samsung announced a 512 megabit PRAM at 60 nanometers, saying that paired with DRAM it could save more than 20% in power. Micron acquired Numonyx in 2010 for about $1.2 billion in stock, and in July 2012 finally shipped 1 gigabit PCM at 45 nanometers, which Nokia put into its Asha feature phones. But in August 2013 Samsung announced mass production of 24-layer 3D NAND, and 3D NAND then set off the steepest cost-decline curve in semiconductor history, and mobile PCM's most compelling rationale was gone. In January 2014 Micron announced it was pulling out of mobile PCM.

17:38 Intel and Micron were split on Optane's positioning from the start
In July 2018 Intel and Micron agreed to a friendly breakup, going their separate ways after completing joint development of the second generation of 3D XPoint. The disagreement was over product direction: Intel initially aimed Optane SSDs at consumer PCs and laptops, hoping to spread wafer costs across volume; Micron wanted to go straight into the data center. Jon Carter hinted back in 2016 that consumer systems did not really need 3D XPoint's low latency, non-volatility and endurance — or at least not enough to pay four to five times the price of NAND for them. In October 2018 Micron announced it would pay $1.5 billion to buy Intel's half of the IM Flash plant in Utah, and Intel shifted to producing it itself.

22:47 Putting Optane in the data center meant redoing motherboards and software
In April 2019 the first DIMM-form-factor Optane DC Persistent Memory went on sale, four years after 3D XPoint was announced, and it required matching Xeon processors, chipsets and motherboards. It had two modes: Memory Mode pooled Optane and DRAM into a single volatile memory pool, working out of the box, but its value depended on DRAM price swings; App Direct Mode was the genuinely valuable mode, letting software write persistent data into Optane so it was still there after a reboot. Restarting an Oracle or SAP database normally takes more than an hour to reload data from SSDs or hard drives, and Optane could eliminate that. One imprecise but directionally useful test showed a 12.5x improvement. But App Direct Mode required programmers to rethink data consistency.

24:51 Only 40% of 582 proofs of concept used the mode that actually mattered
In 2020 Intel updated Optane adoption, saying there were 582 proofs of concept in the pipeline, with SAP HANA and Oracle Exadata the main users and the rest mostly in high-performance computing, infrastructure and some AI analytics. But only 40% used the more valuable App Direct Mode. Intel said it believed the industry would eventually adopt that mode, but it might take years. In the same period Intel announced the sale of its 3D NAND business to SK hynix for $9 billion, with Optane not included in the deal — seemingly an endorsement, but it also let people infer that Optane's implied loss in 2020 was more than $500 million.

25:52 After Micron left, Optane was down to a single supplier
In March 2021 Micron announced it was immediately stopping 3D XPoint development, saying the Utah plant had long suffered from underutilization and dragged $400 million a year off the company, and the plant was later sold to Texas Instruments. Micron attributed the decision to the continuing fall in 3D NAND prices and to the hard changes data centers and applications would have to make to take full advantage of the product. Micron pivoted to betting on the open-standard interface CXL, because machine-learning systems made Micron realize that not just CPUs needed more memory — GPUs and AI accelerator ASICs did too. Micron's public exit severely weakened Optane: customers could rely only on Intel as a single source, and Optane was a proprietary technology. In July 2022, on its earnings call, Intel quietly announced it was shutting down the Optane business.

item.title: Huawei's Ascend chose the hardest road: not compatible with Nvidia
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-touzishizhan-华为昇腾选了一条最难的路-不兼容英伟达/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-touzishizhan-华为昇腾选了一条最难的路-不兼容英伟达/
item.description: For three or four decades Chinese IT has been a follower. Ascend is Huawei's first product that does not solve a choke point but instead walks into uncharted territory, starting at the same time as Nvidia. Xu Zhijun said: anything you do as a follower gets harder and harder the longer you do it.
item.content:encoded:
For three or four decades Chinese IT has been a follower. Ascend is Huawei's first product that does not solve a choke point but instead walks into uncharted territory, starting at the same time as Nvidia. Xu Zhijun said: anything you do as a follower gets harder and harder the longer you do it.

The first half is about how the book was written, with low information density; from the two key decisions at Ascend's founding onward, Fang Xingdong gives a lot of first-hand detail and judgment that only exists in the book.

16:10 Ascend's harshest decision was not being compatible with Nvidia
At Ascend's founding there were two choices. The first was whether AI chips should be specialized or general-purpose; Liao Heng, as chief scientist, judged that AI should be a general-purpose product, and the architecture choice has been proven right today. The second was harder: whether to be compatible with Nvidia. Many domestic chips chose compatibility, with the benefit that Nvidia's existing ecosystem and tools could all be shared. But Xu Zhijun was firm from the start that they had to take a different path. Fang Xingdong believes this choice was extremely bold at the time, and that many times along the way they faced enormous challenges — because the entire Chinese IT industry has been a follower industry for three or four decades, and has never developed based on its own root technology.

19:11 Anything you do as a follower gets harder and harder
Fang Xingdong recalls having dinner with Xu Zhijun three years ago, when Xu Zhijun said, half to himself: Huawei has done this for so many years, and the discovery is that anything you do as a follower always gets harder and harder the longer you do it. There are two kinds of following: in standardized products, Chinese companies can always get closer and closer and even overtake, but by the time they overtake there is no profit left in the industry — 2G to 5G, PCs, phones all went this way; in non-standardized products, such as routers competing with Cisco for so many years, they have not gotten closer. In Xu Zhijun's eyes, what Huawei did in the past was also following. So Ascend is special among the six products: the other five solve choke points and address survival first, while Ascend was not choked in 2019 — it is a completely proactive compute product.

29:16 With process choked off, only system innovation can make it back
Industry chips gain roughly 20%+ performance per generation, mainly from the increase in transistor count driven by advanced process improvements. Huawei lost this premise and can only gain performance through system innovation and breakthroughs — stacked compute, interconnect, higher integration. Fang Xingdong explains with a car metaphor: before, you just had to make the engine stronger and stronger; now the engine is constrained and cannot be enlarged, so you can only make the car run well through architecture, weight reduction, heat dissipation and other factors. Nvidia's solution is to keep working on the engine, because TSMC can still manufacture it. In the interview Liao Heng uses the metaphor of an 18-story pagoda: many companies are good at only one layer because of the great division of labor, while Huawei is forced to do manufacturing, ecosystem and chip design all at once.

34:21 Huawei has to pull the domestic supply chain up with it
Previously Huawei did design, relied on the global supply chain, had TSMC manufacture, could choose the best international partners for other components, directly buy American products and assemble them, sell at a good price with brand premium and decent profit. Now it cannot cooperate abroad, TSMC cannot process for it, and domestic processes are still lacking in every respect, so Huawei has no choice but to support and drive the domestic supply chain — only then does it have a way to survive and get products manufactured. So the challenge of the past seven years is not just improving its own capabilities but also driving the entire supply chain — without driving it, independent autonomy is impossible. Manufacturing is not Huawei's main business, but it has to help companies like SMIC and Yangtze Memory keep advancing process, yield and quality.

37:40 Ascend's significance is not that Huawei survived, but that the industry has an engine
In the past, Huawei's product launches and iterations were still based on American root technology and industrial ecosystem, and the high-value components of a phone were basically foreign. Now Huawei's phones, including Ascend, drive almost 100% domestic supply chains. Fang Xingdong believes the greatest significance of the Tao Dinglü is not that Huawei itself can survive and be autonomous, but that China's entire semiconductor industry and entire IT industry have their own engine, which never existed before. Huawei's rapid development represents the rapid development of the entire industrial ecosystem. He also points out that the market, looking at reports, news or public opinion, has not yet realized that we are at this inflection point in the cycle — mention Nvidia and people think it is formidable, mention Huawei and they say it is policy that makes people use it.

45:47 It is not a question of difficulty, but of cognition and resolve
Fang Xingdong believes doing communications versus doing IT is essentially not a question of difficulty but of cognition and resolve — whether you dare to do it. The most typical example is the Gauss database: among these six products Ascend stood out, and the least conspicuous is probably Gauss, but the database is a half-century-old industry with a relatively stable market, and being choked on it would be deadly. At the time Huawei wanted to acquire or support domestic vendors, but after research found none of them were up to it; domestic companies could only grow in the cracks of American giants, with small scale, weak R&D capability and weak product innovation. So Huawei decided to do it itself, benchmarking Oracle, and from 2011 and 2012 invested 1 billion, 2 billion, 3 billion yuan a year, without knowing whether there would be any output in the future.

1:06:04 The future is two centers, not one replacing the other
Fang Xingdong judges that the shift of global high tech from a single system centered on the US to two centers is the general trend; politics will not allow a continued single center — the US will not allow it, and China will not allow it either. He believes a single center is itself abnormal, and only two centers can create competition — only with two systems does every consumer, every company, every country, no matter how big or small, have a choice, and not be choked into a forced either-or. So the mission of Huawei's six products is to go from being the second choice to being the better choice; the relationship with Nvidia is not simple substitution but each having its strengths, complementing each other, and coopetition. He admits the American system is currently stronger, with its advantage mainly in advanced manufacturing, and that Huawei, under process constraints, relies on the Tao Dinglü not to be left behind; once advanced process is also broken through, it can work both ways at once.

1:19:11 The tech war won in the short term, at a greater long-term cost
Fang Xingdong believes the US did indeed suppress Huawei through the tech war, but cannot solve the problem in the long term. He reasons: without the national confrontation of 2017 and 2018, Huawei might be at least one-third of Nvidia and one-third of Apple, possibly China's largest company by market cap; in 2019 Huawei had already surpassed Apple, and its global shipments briefly surpassed Samsung for one quarter. Nvidia today is dominant alone; if it had been running neck and neck with Huawei in AI chips from the start, it could not have reached this position today. He judges that once the side being attacked builds a self-cycle that does not rely on the outside, and the other side cannot eliminate it even under the harshest conditions, it will be even harder to eliminate later; it will only grow stronger, turning from one monopoly into two competitors.

item.title: Ads Are Machine Learning 1.0: How AppLovin Earned an 84% Margin
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-allin-广告是机器学习的-1-0-applovin-靠它赚出-84-利润率/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-allin-广告是机器学习的-1-0-applovin-靠它赚出-84-利润率/
item.description: Advertising isn't AI's past tense — it's the earliest and most profitable deployment of deep learning. AppLovin used recommendation models to build an 84% EBITDA margin in the $50 billion mobile game ad market, and became its own best investor with $6 billion in buybacks.
item.content:encoded:
Advertising isn't AI's past tense — it's the earliest and most profitable deployment of deep learning. AppLovin used recommendation models to build an 84% EBITDA margin in the $50 billion mobile game ad market, and became its own best investor with $6 billion in buybacks.

A CEO who almost never gives interviews explains the shared technical roots of ads and AI, the buyback playbook through a 92% drawdown, and why a Chinese engineering team is an advantage. High information density, worth listening to.

1:02 Mobile game advertising is a $50 billion market
Adam says outsiders underestimate the scale of mobile gaming: more than a billion adults play casual mobile games every day, and these people are household decision-makers. Two years ago AppLovin disclosed $11 billion in annual ad spend on its own platform, and it has grown roughly 60% year over year since, which by rough math puts it around $20 billion today. But that isn't the whole market — many other ad companies monetize in this ecosystem, so double that number and the entire mobile gaming ecosystem spends roughly $50 billion a year on advertising. He notes that not long ago social was also just a $50 billion opportunity.

3:02 Advertising is machine learning's earliest and most profitable deployment
Adam calls advertising ML 1.0: it was the first deployment of all the technology that now drives AI. Large language models create more economic value today than advertising, but advertising is an extremely profitable deployment of deep learning models. Recommendation systems and large language models differ in architecture, but their trajectories are highly similar — research in large language models transfers to recommendation systems and vice versa; many LLM researchers spent the early part of their careers looking at ad systems. The beauty of the ad business is that you build a model to predict a future outcome, and the value of that prediction can be converted into money immediately.

6:03 Search ads create no economic expansion; discovery ads do
Adam splits advertising into two categories. One is bottom-of-funnel advertising: the consumer already knows what they want to buy and is just doing research to complete the transaction — that's Google Search's business, and large language models will compete with Google Search almost entirely there. The other is his category: not knowing user intent, and creating demand that didn't exist so the user sees something and thinks ‘this looks really cool, I want to buy it right now’. He stresses that the transaction in search or in an LLM would have happened anyway, so there isn't much economic expansion there; discovery advertising creates economic expansion, which is what makes Meta's ad business strong and what AppLovin wants to do.

8:07 Your phone isn't listening, but your behavior is tracked
Faced with the question of ‘I mention something at lunch and then an ad shows up’, Adam says it's more likely you did something trackable earlier — a search, browsing a website, searching for a product — without realizing it, and then you said something related and started seeing related ads. He states plainly that AppLovin does not track location at all, arguing that tracking precise location to render ads is a very heavy concept, and that the data transfer required to parse microphone content in real time and translate it into ads isn't realistic. But he concedes that if you're on a social network, relationship data between you and others can of course drive the ad experience — for example, a friend searched for something and you might see a related ad, which he thinks is fine.

10:07 From $28 billion to $3.8 billion, then it started buying itself
AppLovin went public in April 2021 with $600 million in EBITDA at a market cap of about $28 billion, peaking at $40 billion. In 2022 the stock fell almost every day, down to a market cap of about $3.8 billion — in a year when the company did $1 billion in EBITDA. Adam's read: market cap is determined by the quality of investors, and a lot of companies went public at the same time, so blue-chip investors didn't do the research to figure out what this company with the silly name was; the result was no demand and lots of supply, and the valuation fell from 50x EBITDA to under 4x. His response was to stop talking to investors and instead buy back aggressively with the large amounts of cash the company generated; since then it has bought roughly $6 billion of its own stock and retired 20% to 25% of shares outstanding.

12:07 When the stock fell 92%, family called to ask if you were suicidal
Adam says that period was hard, that family and friends would call to ask if he was suicidal, and his answer was that the stock was still at $10 and had still gone up a lot. But the truly hard part was realizing that as CEO, his team was getting the same calls, and they didn't have his composure or his equity. So they rallied the team around a ‘we versus the world’ mentality, and extended a performance stock program usually reserved for the CEO to key people across the company, telling them: it's hard right now, the house you thought you had is gone, but if you hold on and recover, the upside is huge. Later investors started coming back, the company switched from regression models to deep learning models, the ad algorithm got better, advertiser returns got better, and the business started growing fast.

14:08 One week in New York took the market cap from $28 billion to $55 billion
When the new model launched in April 2023 the company still wasn't talking to investors, so the outside world didn't know. By around September 2023 the stock was at $80 with good results, and Adam judged the market cap high enough that it couldn't buy back that aggressively anymore, so he went to New York and started talking to investors. In that one week the stock went from $80 to $150 and the market cap went from $28 billion to $55 billion — just because he went out and said ‘our company is still here, we survived’. He describes sitting in meetings and being able to read the person across the table texting a friend to buy. Over the next two and a half years the stock went from $9 to $750, a $250 billion market cap. His conclusion is that public market investors and private investors aren't that different — they all chase trends, just often later than you'd like.

16:09 After privacy rules tightened, users complained ads got worse
Adam says in these areas you want regulatory clarity, and once the rules are clear, technology can respond. Five years ago you could target users precisely on iOS; today, if users say no precise targeting, you can only bundle them into groups and serve worse ads. The interesting result of that change was that after Apple's changes the company got a flood of user complaints saying ‘show me more relevant ads, you're showing me a bunch of junk now’. So he offers a duality: on one hand you need privacy regulation so tech companies know what to do, on the other hand consumers genuinely want relevant ads — when you watch a 30-second ad in a game to get an extra life, you're getting something with monetary value, and you don't want to spend those 30 seconds on junk.

item.title: Buffets Weren't Eaten to Death — They Were Hollowed Out by the Supermarket Deli
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-modernmba-自助餐不是被吃垮的-是被超市熟食区掏空的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-modernmba-自助餐不是被吃垮的-是被超市熟食区掏空的/
item.description: The 1980s buffet was propped up by cheap ingredients, cheap land, cheap labor and stagnant wages. When all four inputs got more expensive, what actually killed it was the supermarket deli eating the low-price market at zero customer-acquisition cost.
item.content:encoded:
The 1980s buffet was propped up by cheap ingredients, cheap land, cheap labor and stagnant wages. When all four inputs got more expensive, what actually killed it was the supermarket deli eating the low-price market at zero customer-acquisition cost.

It dissects one industry's cause of death using the financials and bankruptcy filings of three public companies — the mechanism is clear and the numbers are solid, and the back half on supermarket deli counters is the most valuable part.

0:02 The buffet deleted everything hard about running a restaurant
The real leap of the 1980s buffet was upgrading "unlimited" from a side dish to the entire business model. It cut every hard part of a traditional restaurant: no servers to hire, no menu to design, barely any English required, no precision needed. The only job was cooking in bulk, heating frozen appetizers and portioning factory cake. Compared with a conventional restaurant where every dish has to earn back its own price, a buffet only has to keep the trays full. Lower skill threshold, a concept that sells itself, one family able to run the whole kitchen, customers serving themselves — the whole model ran on volume. Within a decade, nearly every small town in the Midwest had a Chinese buffet.

8:07 Opening restaurants and keeping customers are two different businesses
Buffets Inc.'s Old Country and Hometown had the simplest strategy: this model doesn't need improvement, it needs replication. From one store to 200 in a decade, doubling again in five years, at its peak opening more than one a week, and after the 1996 merger the largest and fastest buffet operator in the world with nearly a billion dollars in annual revenue. But fast success created a fatal blind spot — they built the muscle for opening buffets, not the muscle for keeping customers. The two chains had no real brand, no signature dish, no trademarked recipe; they competed only on price and on the volume rather than the quality of their advertising. The company bet everything on "scale itself compounds," and 17% restaurant-level margins in the early 1990s meant nobody dared question the playbook.

9:07 Same-store sales fell for five straight years and nobody knew why
In 1994 same-store sales turned negative and stayed red for five consecutive years; sales were flat for over a decade and trailed inflation. Nothing about the restaurants themselves had changed: nearly 40% of the two chains' locations had been opened or remodeled in the previous two years, price increases were small, and after the merger there was no competitor left. But the traffic simply stopped coming, as if Americans had suddenly had enough starting in the mid-1990s, and the format and the chains' novelty faded for no clear reason. The company tried fix after fix, all of them one-year band-aids: in 1995 it cut advertising below 1% of sales to buy profit, and the next year posted the worst same-store sales in its history; only tripling the ad budget turned same-store sales positive — meaning it had to keep marketing and sacrifice margin just to get people through the door.

11:07 Six years under private equity and traffic never improved once
In 2000 a New York private equity firm borrowed more than $500 million to take Buffets Inc. private, and the spreadsheet logic was beautiful: cut costs, maximize earnings, cover the acquisition debt's interest with cash flow, squeeze the remaining customers dry, then repackage it for an IPO. But over the six-year holding period traffic never improved. The firm immediately raised prices, cut staff and service, then compensated with promotions, which only alienated customers further and eroded margin. By 2005 the once-healthy company was stuffed with debt, the firm had taken $90 million in dividends for itself, and what was left was a shell paying lenders more in interest than the restaurants earned. Buying Ryan's was just a bigger dose of the same disease — the money came from selling off the land under most of Ryan's restaurants, turning the only asset that didn't depend on traffic into a new annual rent bill.

15:09 No meat was Fresh Choice's profit itself
Fresh Choice tried to solve the economics from the other end: replace expensive protein, which drives up food cost, with cheap salads and carbs. It charged the same prices in Northern California as Old Country and Hometown did in Ohio, yet its food cost stayed 10% below its competitors' — and that gap was the entire profit. But customers consistently refused to pay more without a real main course, and every investment meant to justify a price increase only accelerated the churn. The company couldn't give in either, because "no meat" was precisely where its profit came from. It tried uniform pricing, eliminating discounts, adding chicken to the salad, launching thicker soups, designing smaller and cheaper new store formats — none of it worked. By the late 1990s, falling traffic plus a complete lack of pricing power dragged the company into annual losses and penny-stock territory.

21:14 Even the most efficient operator went down all the same
Sweet Tomatoes was the most efficient, most disciplined operator in the industry, and it still came apart. From the start it made itself a destination: standalone restaurants with private parking on land it owned, rather than renting in strip malls like its rivals. Each store had a 55-foot salad bar, eight made-from-scratch soups, a baked potato bar, a dessert bar, a pasta station and a bakery, and since the 1980s it pushed signature items like tuna tarragon and Joan's broccoli madness — branded dishes that injected crucial credibility. On siting it picked business districts and near shopping centers that could capture both lunch and dinner, bought land where it could and otherwise locked in 30-year leases. It also centralized on both the prep and store ends, building 19 central kitchens to make food in bulk and distribute it to each store, and during expansion it placed new stores near central kitchens to keep capacity utilized. But logic and discipline only delayed the inevitable.

24:14 What killed the buffet was the supermarket deli counter
The way the three giants died was no coincidence: Fresh Choice had the cheapest food cost and died because customers wouldn't pay more than $7 for dinner; Sweet Tomatoes ran the most efficiently and survived as long as it did only because it owned the land under its restaurants; Buffets Inc. had the most locations, the cheapest labor and the strongest economies of scale, and still couldn't raise prices without losing customers. And the fast food and casual chains that had piggybacked on the 1980s were the first to draw the conclusion — by the late 1990s Wendy's, Burger King and KFC had all shut down their salad bars and unlimited bundles, because none of them made money. The real killer came from inside the supermarket: frozen meals never disrupted the buffet, because they're single-serving while the buffet was designed for families; but dinner simply moved to the deli counter of that same supermarket. The supermarket doesn't need the deli to support the whole store, it prices by the pound and by the piece, customers already come in weekly for milk and eggs, and the deli is a cross-sell at zero customer-acquisition cost that also shares labor and overhead.

30:22 The buffet couldn't pull a single one of its four profit levers
Every restaurant has only four levers to profit: raise prices, shrink portions, cut labor, shrink the footprint. The buffet chains had none of them. They couldn't raise prices, couldn't cut labor, couldn't shrink portions, couldn't shrink the restaurant. Since the 1990s the whole restaurant industry has moved toward "do more in less space," but a buffet can never be truly efficient — it needs those square feet to hold the variety that makes it appealing, and once it opens big it has to stay big. That worked in the 1980s, when land was cheap, malls were sprouting everywhere and landlords cared more about traffic than rent. But as malls fell out of favor, retail migrated and e-commerce hollowed out the strip centers, these chains found themselves locked into 10,000-square-foot boxes nobody wanted. That's why all the chains filed Chapter 11 again and again — bankruptcy was the only legal way to escape hundreds of leases no one else would take.

item.title: More Collaboration, Slower System: Counterintuitive Management from the Product Chiefs at Snap and Discord
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-lennys-协作越多越慢-snap-和-discord-产品一号位反直觉管理法/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-lennys-协作越多越慢-snap-和-discord-产品一号位反直觉管理法/
item.description: Collaboration has hidden costs nobody has internalized, and coordination costs guarantee you can only move as fast as the slowest node in the system. So Peter Sellis deliberately and aggressively internalizes the cost of collaboration, rather than defaulting to more-is-better.
item.content:encoded:
Collaboration has hidden costs nobody has internalized, and coordination costs guarantee you can only move as fast as the slowest node in the system. So Peter Sellis deliberately and aggressively internalizes the cost of collaboration, rather than defaulting to more-is-better.

High information density, but the back half is worth more than the front half. For people who want to hear how a product leader actually makes decisions, not for people who want specific growth playbooks.

6:07 More collaboration makes the system slower
Peter says you will never hear an executive say ‘stop collaborating’, and to him that is precisely a warning sign. Collaboration brings enormous coordination costs, and coordination costs guarantee you can only move as fast as the slowest node in the system. So he deliberately and aggressively internalizes the cost of collaboration, rather than defaulting to more-is-better. This is also where his ‘design teams like a terrorist organization’ idea comes from: one ideological culture that makes everyone understand why we're doing this, plus a very clear organizational structure specifying who can be trusted with which decision. With those two things, you don't need to over-collaborate and you still get results that feel like you did.

16:12 The median PM gap is a math-structure problem
Peter offers a distributional explanation: product management ability is normally distributed in the population, and the people who actually become PMs are cut from the right tail; once you cut it, it becomes a power-law distribution, and the median of a power-law distribution is far below the mean. Layer on two more mechanisms: in the ZERP era it became the most lucrative career in tech for people without a technical background, and the definition is subjective, so the people who get in have extremely strong incentives to stay; meanwhile the genuinely strong ones have skills that map almost perfectly onto other executive roles or starting their own company, so ‘great product managers are exiting the system’. Squeezed from both ends, the median is naturally bad. He also points out that the people actually complaining about PMs are the middle cohort of engineers — great engineers know how to bend a PM into the shape they want, and terrible engineers can hide behind the PM's decisions.

21:16 Snap's ads couldn't scale for three mathematical reasons
First, the user base is extremely young, and between 17 and 18, and between 18 and 21, there is a ‘suspicious discontinuity’ in ad CPMs both inside and outside the US; the rules for tracking, measuring and targeting under-17s are extremely strict, and what's hard to measure is hard to build performance products around. Second, almost all non-search display advertising opens on a screen that exists to show ads, whereas Snap opens a camera — in the core flow of taking a snap and sending it to a friend, there's no logical place to put an ad; it's a creation-oriented product, not a consumption-oriented one. Third, it is fundamentally a messaging app, and there is currently no good messaging ad product; Asian chat apps get cited over and over, but break it down by dollars spent per unit of time and none of them does particularly well.

35:25 Taste is the nerve to leave good things on the shelf
Peter says one thing he learned at Snap: he watched Evan say no to better ideas than almost anything any other consumer startup has ever shipped. He describes the product leader's goal as turning the founder into the world's richest museum curator — what's on display in the product right now is only a small fraction of the whole collection, the pieces the curator judges right for this time and place. He offers a way to probe taste in interviews: ask what the person built but never shipped — not something killed because the data was bad, but something they held as a prototype and then judged ‘the world isn't ready’ or ‘this thing isn't ready’. If a museum hangs its entire collection on the walls, the curator has done nothing.

40:29 Advertising is the internet's product-market fit
Peter comes down squarely on Eric Seufert's side: advertising is the internet's product-market fit, and subscription consumer products are overrated. He judges OpenAI to have ‘last mover advantage’ in ads — Meta already solved modern ad auctions as a ‘solved problem’ from 2010 to 2020, and OpenAI is just running through each component fast. Mechanically he names the modified VCG (Vickrey-Clarke-Groves) auction: the highest bidder doesn't win; instead the advertiser's natural value for that user is folded into the bid, so a high bidder who wants to reach people who don't want to be reached has to pay more. This mechanism lets organic content and ad content sit in the same auction, with dollars as the common denominator.

42:30 In chat, the denominator for ads is trust, not relevance
Peter replaces ‘natural value’ in VCG with ‘trust’ in the chat context. A user asks ‘which microphone should I buy’, and the product has to decide whether to give an objective answer, a set of answers, or an advertiser-influenced one — and the degree of influence should equal how much trust you're willing to trade away. He uses Amazon search as an example: search for something and you scroll past 16 ads before the first real result, which subtly erodes users' trust in the system. So OpenAI's real deciding factor isn't whether to do ads, but how to mathematically maximize long-term trust inside the auction mechanism — trust maximization is very likely correlated with retention, possibly even causal.

50:35 Growth comes from the core, not from new markets
Verified twice, at Snap and at Discord: a network-effects business already wants to grow, and the most effective move is to serve better — faster, more relevantly — the people already using the product, or wanting to use it, for what it's actually for. He explains with eighth-grade math: it takes 30 monthly actives to equal one daily active, so consumer products should optimize the DAU/MAU ratio; moving that ratio a few basis points is far more worthwhile than pulling in a pile of new MAUs and gambling on retention. Snap's lesson came from the disastrous 2018 redesign, the only quarter Snap's overall DAU went flat quarter-over-quarter; after that the team ground away at Android performance, producing a multi-year growth revival. Discord's version is more counterintuitive: at the time Midjourney was built on Discord and outsiders all thought this was Discord's big opportunity, but Peter says if you pull up the Discord usage curve, you simply cannot pick out the Midjourney segment.

1:02:44 SpaceX is burning its own ships on purpose
Peter considers SpaceX the greatest company right now, and the most instructive thing is how it fights the future: Falcon 9 is the world's best reusable launch system, other countries would trade GDP for it, and yet SpaceX announced it will stop selling Falcon 9 seats in a few years and pivot to Starship. He calls it a Cortez-level burning of the ships, a way to avoid what Christensen called the innovator's dilemma — because even holding the best thing, you're still willing to build the thing that makes your current product irrelevant. He also notes that SpaceX and Tesla publish ten-year plans on their websites, and Tesla even open-sources its patents; that confidence — ‘I'll tell you what to do, and if you think you can do it better, come copy it’ — is what he aspires to as a product leader.

item.title: Paying Hip-Hop's Pioneers, and They Thought It Was a Scam
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-a16z-给嘻哈元老发钱-他们以为是诈骗/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-a16z-给嘻哈元老发钱-他们以为是诈骗/
item.description: Some didn't even show up to collect, because they didn't believe it was real. In hip-hop you can't just hand someone money — as Nas put it, you have to give recognition and dignity first, and only then can the money be accepted.
item.content:encoded:
Some didn't even show up to collect, because they didn't believe it was real. In hip-hop you can't just hand someone money — as Nas put it, you have to give recognition and dignity first, and only then can the money be accepted.

This isn't an investment interview; it's a roundtable on how to pay back a debt owed to a culture. Worth hearing if you care about distribution mechanisms in the creator economy, or if you want to know what Ben Horowitz is actually busy with in private.

2:04 A $10 album owed $5 million
The starting point is a debt Ben Horowitz owed himself: he once paid $10 for the Paid in Full album, and over his career he got at least $5 million of value out of that record, with no channel to pay it back — and he felt he had to. He called Steve Stoute first, and Steve said the idea was not only good but timely: everyone was saying these old rappers were broke and dusty, but nobody was actually doing anything. The second call went to Nas, who said Quincy Jones's Jazz Foundation model wouldn't work in hip-hop: you can't just give a person money, it has to be recognition of what he did and who he is, and it has to be more than money. So the shape became an awards ceremony and a Grandmaster Award, with Scarface and Rakim in the first class of honorees.

5:05 Some thought it was a scam and didn't come collect
The foundation's first obstacle wasn't money, it was that nobody believed it. Ben says the early disbelief was beyond what you'd imagine, and for a while they had real trouble actually getting money into people's hands — some didn't even show up to accept the award because they thought it was a scam, and others said, "I don't need anyone giving me money." He treats that disbelief as evidence the design was right: it can't look like reparations, it has to be celebration and tribute, shining the light they're owed on them, and only then will it be accepted. Caz later put it more bluntly: the industry has shortchanged these people for so long that the first reaction can only be "why would anyone help us now."

10:07 The first hip-hop hit was stolen from him
Grandmaster Caz wrote the rhyme that became Rapper's Delight, his own name was even in the rhyme, and the first hip-hop hit was taken out of his hands just like that, with nothing coming back to him. Ben says everyone in the music industry knows this, but nobody ever did anything, and nobody ever said anything. The first time he met Caz in New York he was stunned: this is a man who changes the energy of any room he walks into today, and he carries no bitterness at all, still thinking of himself as a star. Steve added: it's not that nobody knows, it's that not enough people know — the industry knows, the public doesn't.

17:10 Dr. Dre asked for an introduction to his idol
Steve Stoute tells a detail: Dr. Dre heard about Paid in Full and decided to come, then asked whether Steve could introduce him to Kool Moe Dee — Dre had never met him. Another time, in Las Vegas, Dre again asked to be introduced to Slick Rick, whom he had also never met. A Dre who has made it has to ask for an introduction to meet these legends, which shows how fragmented the scene is — and getting these people into one room happened only because of this foundation. Caz puts it more directly: the industry separates people by success, status, and who's hot; for years he only ran into Nas by chance, and now they see each other once a year and can call each other.

32:20 The Grammys botched it, so they did it themselves
Quincy Jones was the legend of legends to this group, but when he died the Grammy tribute was called, flatly, botched. The Quincy Jones Award wasn't conceived to fill a slot; it came from seeing the Grammys get it wrong, and Quincy's son QD3 saying fine, we'll do it ourselves — that's how it became a fixed annual award from the foundation. This year's recipient is Nile Rodgers. Steve mentions that George Clinton showed up last year with his "mothership" prop and, at 83, recited the lyrics to Rakim's "Follow the Leader" on stage — a man who changed music, paying tribute to another man who changed music.

39:24 Hip-hop has no social security
Caz explained what the money concretely means: a grant paid out over five years, with which he bought a house and moved out of the projects. He lived his whole life in the Bronx, and for the past ten to fifteen years his last thought at night was always "I don't want to die in the projects"; now he and his wife live in a house in Pennsylvania. He says hip-hop has no social security and no health insurance, you have to keep working, which is why you still see him doing radio, playing parks, doing hip-hop tours — because he has to. The money gave him something he'd never had: a buffer. He also made a point of saying money is only part of it; the real thing is being put in the light.

44:26 Brands came back from the dead on hip-hop
Steve Stoute uses business data to argue why "paying the debt" is justified: Adidas had only 2% of the US market at the time, three-quarters of it from the Northeast, and the company just saw a bunch of people frantically buying the same shoe and throwing the laces away, with no idea why. Grand Puba's line "First things first, obey your thirst" later became Sprite's ad slogan. Tommy Hilfiger was selling ties that wouldn't move; driving through Harlem he saw everyone wearing their pants low with the Calvin Klein waistband showing, went back and made his own waistband wider and thicker with his name on it, and only then did the brand take off. These brands exist because of what these people contributed.

48:31 Love isn't writing a check, it's flying to Houston
Ben tells a story about his wife, who is also the foundation's chair, Felicia, to illustrate how this organization differs from other philanthropy: Scarface had a heart problem and needed open-heart surgery, but he came from a place where people barely even go to the doctor, he was afraid to go, and on the phone he said he wasn't going. Felicia flew to Houston and said no, you're going now. Just as they walked into the exam room, his aorta ruptured, and the doctors got him in in time and saved his life. Steve adds the everyday version: she'll suddenly call to ask how you and your family are doing, and if someone in your family gets sick, flowers show up the next day, or whatever was agreed shows up.

item.title: Fashion Mogul: Stop Apologizing for Being a Working Mom, and Talk About Money
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-wsjournal-时尚大亨-当妈不必道歉-钱要开口谈/
